I can make a statement now as
to the progress that has been made. The government of the province of New Brunswick advised that after investigation they had not sufficient evidence to warrant them in going ahead with any criminal charge, and left it to the military authorities to take such steps as they thought advisable. The military authorities immediately reconvened the court of inquiry; as a matter of fact I think there were some new officers on it from headquarters, in order to elicit the facts as fully as possible, not only with regard to the shooting incident but also with regard to the matter of discipline. speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: OPERATIONS IN SICILY-OFFICER IN CHARGE OF CANADIAN FORCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not sorry the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) has asked the question he has just asked. I should like to supplement what my colleague the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) has said, by a word with respect to making announcements on the progress of the war, on matters pertaining to our own troops in particular, and also on many matters which pertain to Canada's participation in the war.
I wish to say quite frankly that repeatedly I find myself in extremely difficult positions. From time to time, along with others, I have received confidential information as to what was about to take place, so that I might be fully informed. But I have also at the same time received word that this information on no account was to be released until receipt of further word. Such further word does not always come as rapidly as one might like it to come.
There is the fact that other nations, and other parts of the empire, are also engaged in this war. They also have troops on active service, and in some instances, of necessity, announcements have therefore to be restricted to those who are recognized as being in supreme control of the direction of the war. I believe we are all only too ready and too happy to recognize that the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, Mr. Churchill, and the President of the United States, Mr. Roosevelt, are the two men to whom all parts of the united nations and of the empire look as the two who have under their control the supreme direction of the war. Announcements will undoubtedly from time to time be made by these two gentlemen. Members of the house and people throughout Canada may say to themselves that it is rather singular that the Prime Minister of Canada has not

War Appropriation-Finance-Wool Board
made an announcement on this point, seeing that Canadian forces are so immediately involved and concerned. I have to choose between recognizing that other parts of the empire and others of the united nations would not wish to have Canada placed in a position more favourable than that which they occupy in connection with announcements of the kind, and leave those announcements either to Mr. Churchill, to the President or to both, or- as the other alternative-make a fuss about it, and see if the matter cannot be changed. I have felt that at least one of the greatest services I could render to all concerned at this time is to find as little fault as I can, and do as much as I can to avoid embarrassment. From time to time I have had to take that position, at the risk of great misunderstanding.
I do not mind telling the house, now that the event has passed, that all day Friday I had full knowledge of what was being planned. I was waiting for an opportunity to make an announcement on Friday, and until eleven o'clock at night I had hoped to be able to make it before the house adjourned. I had received a communication pointing out that for reasons of security no mention was to be made at all of the participation of the Canadian forces. And I might say that it was even contrary to the request I had received that no word was to be given respecting the participation of the Canadian forces in the invasion of Sicily until late Saturday-I say it was in spite of that that I made the announcement shortly after midnight on Friday. I made it because an announcement that Canadian troops were involved came, over the air, from military headquarters in the United States.
In justice to myself, and with a view to possible future situations, I feel I should make it clear that sometimes we in Canada are placed in very difficult positions. Let it be understood that I am not criticizing anyone. I do say that perhaps those who felt reasons of security would demand that there should be no mention of the participation of Canadian troops took that position for the best. But I have been asking myself what the House of Commons and the country would have had to say about the Prime Minister of Canada if he had not made any mention of the participation by Canadian troops in the attack upon Sicily until midnight on Saturday, instead of making it immediately after midnight on Friday.

With
respect to the price of wool and the index figure which the minister gave, I think the whole picture ought to be shown. In 1917 the United States was not in the war. The wool trade on the north American continent is centred in the United States. Boston is the great mart for the whole of North America. There was much inflation in the United States owing to largely increased buying power, resulting largely from the mass of treasure which was poured into the United States by Britain for the purchase of armaments. There was no control of prices in the United States, and prices in Canada, without any control over there, naturally had to soar to a point commensurate with the level in the United States. When my hon. friends across the way are drawing comparisons between prices today and prices in the last war of the same articles, they should never lose sight of the fact that conditions are entirely dissimilar. I commend to hon. gentlemen the reading of a letter written by Sir Thomas White which appeared in the Toronto Globe and Mail a few weeks ago, setting out clearly the whole position. We have to keep it in mind. The intention of course is to show how much better the Murphys are than the O'Rourkes.

I should like to read figures showing prices paid in Canada and the United States during the past few years. They have been given to me by Mr. W. S. Benson, of the Southern Alberta Sheep Breeders Association, whose headquarters are at Lethbridge, a man who I believe is quite dependable. The following prices per pound obtained: The United States between 1930 and 1939 was paying on the average 23-6 cents, and Canada was paying 10-59 cents. In 1939 United States was paying 22-3 cents while Canada was paying 11-8 cents-much to be proud of, our country has! The average price for 1942 in the United States was 39 cents, and in Canada 25-9 cents. So that with all the great percentage increase in prices of -wool to Canadian producers, they still were being neglected as compared with their fellow wool producers across the line. The increase in the United States over 1939 was only 74-4 per cent; the increase in Canada was 119-4 per cent, but even at that, the United States was paying in 1942 practically 14 cents per pound more for wool than Canada was. I think the minister will recognize that these figures disclose a situation which is not to the credit of the Canadian wool board. It is a situation which it is difficult to find language to describe adequately.
I am going to give a few more figures for the minister to think about. I have here from the same gentleman, Mr. Benson, a set of prices taken from the books of a Manitoba sheep grower. These prices go back over the years. The 1923 price was 20-6 cents. The 1924 price was evidently not recorded. Then follow: 1925, 22-4 cents; 1926, 16-1 cents; 1927, 19-8 cents; 1928, 33-7 cents; 1929, 16-5 cents; 1930, 7-5 cents; 1931, 3 cents. I believe the wool board would at least have done itself justice had it taken into consideration some such matters as these, but evidently it did not. I continue: 1932, 3-1 cents; 1933, 12-1 cents; 1934. 6-7 cents; 1935, 12 cents; 1936, 14-5 cents; 1937, 13-8 cents; 1938, 10-7 cents; 1939, 15-6 cents; 1940, 19-8 cents; 1941, 24-3 cents; 1942, 27-1 cents. This return of course is based on Manitoba conditions. I believe the minister himself will be astonished to find that such a set of prices prevailed in Canada. I am not blaming the minister; probably it has never been brought to his attention what questionable practices his wool board have been guilty of during the last year or so.
I am going to draw to his attention one or two other small matters which probably will be food for thought. In the first place I notice he said that the price for wool in 1943 was to be the same as the price for wool in 1942. Has it been brought to his attention -he is an exceedingly busy man and probably

War Appropriation-
-Finance-
-Wool Board
it has not-how greatly the costs of producing wool have increased during the last year?
I have here a letter dated March 16, 1943, from the gentleman to whom I referred a moment ago, Mr. W. S. Benson, secretary-treasurer of Southern Alberta Sheep Breeders Limited, in which he points out to me several important increases in the cost of producing wool. In the first place the 1942 wages for farm help have increased tremendously, in some cases as much as 100 per cent. The growers would be prepared to pay these increased wages if they were obtaining increased efficiency, but unfortunately the reverse is the case, because experienced men are very difficult to obtain. One has to rely on inexperienced and inefficient help. ' This fact, however, did not register with the wool board although it was brought forcibly to their attention. Secondly, "The cost per head of shearing has practically doubled during the last two years and growers feel that the coming season they will have to pay a 25 per cent increase in order to get their shearing done." That is another matter that did not register with the representatives of the wool board when they visited Lethbridge.
What is the cost of shearing?

I have a letter in
which it is given, but I cannot state it offhand. I read again:
During the present winter, ranchers have been put to much more expense than usual on account of the long feeding periods as a result of the unfavourable winter.
That is another point which apparently entirely escaped the doctrinaires who have been called to responsible positions on the Canadian wool board, men who apparently have no contacts with the producers. The fourth point is this. The people generally in the Lethbridge area-and, if I am correctly informed, all through Alberta and other parts of the west-asked that the price be increased at least ten cents per pound over what they received in 1942. I know that this request was made of the representatives of the wool board at Lethbridge and was completely disregarded, in many cases without much respect being shown.
This quotation is important:
The present income tax schedule as outlined in the budget does not give the rancher a chance to pay off his debt, even if he were so inclined.
I do not wish to take up the time of the committee by reading the minister a lecture on the inequities and the injustice of his income tax structure, but I will draw that statement to his attention with the request that he think it over before he builds his
next budget. The minister, in fixing his income tax rates for the sheep growers in Canada, made no allowance at all for the tremendous losses suffered and the debts incurred by sheep growers when they were passing through the dreadful times in which they received 3 cents, 3-1 cents and 6-7 cents per pound. He simply clamped on a tax that would ruin them, and if the war goes on for five or six or seven years, and the men continue to be treated as they are at the present time under the income tax, the minister will squeeze them out of existence. If that is what he wants to do, he is on the high road to the achievement of his goal.
These matters are weighty; they have been entirely overlooked by the wool board, which has been travelling around the country and telling the farmers what they ought to be able to do. I would call the minister's attention to this fact. The main wool producers, the representatives of sheep producers' organizations, have been outspoken on this question of price in several parts of Canada. I would refer the minister to a little publication called "Country Life in British Columbia," of March, 1943, at page 16, wherein there is printed an article entitled "Words from President Harrison re treatment of B.C. sheep industry." In the fifth line of the first paragraph these words are attributed to Mr. Harrison:
Bluntly he states that the producers of wool were not receiving a fair price for this essential commodity,'that the price of lambs had been reduced unduly last summer, and that if the dominion government's urgent request for the raising of a million more sheep in Canada was to be satisfied, something had to be done about assuring a supply of labour, prices in line with costs of production, and protection against predatory animals.
We have nothing to do with the first and last of the list at this stage, but we have a good deal to do with the matter of price. I call attention too to an article in "Country Life in British Columbia," March, 1943, at page 17:	"Wool price too low, so sheep
breeders charge." I quote from the second main article on the page:
At the annual meeting of the Ontario Sheep Breeders' Association, about the only complaint heard was that the price of wool was too low. The sheep breeders thought they should have 50 cents a pound.
In order to get some idea of the situation, all the minister has to do is to compare 50 cents a pound with the contemptible 25^4 which now is paid. If it were a purely western voice speaking, the voice of British Columbia, probably the officials at Ottawa would use their habitual restraint towards that province. But here is a statement from Ontario which

War Appropriation-Finance-Wool Board
should sound loud in the ears of the men at Ottawa. How a statement like this could have missed the attention of members of the wool board, I am not at the moment able to conjecture. May I also call attention to an article which appears in the Farm and Ranch Review of January, 1943. This article appears under the title, " Sheep industry is stifled," and is written by T. C. Glaspell, vice-president of the Canadian Sheep Breeders' association. It was written for the Farmers' Advocate and is quoted in the Farm and Ranch Review. I would call attention particularly to the words near the end of the article:
I challenge our agricultural supply board to prove to the sheep breeders of Canada that wool can be raised under 50 cents per pound under present conditions.
We have here two voices, each one estimating 50 cents as the lowest suitable price. The Alberta request to raise the price ten cents a pound is in the light of the other two exceedingly moderate, and should have merited some respect from the visiting wool board representatives. But it did not.
In view of these statements the minister would be well advised to call the chairman of the wool board on the carpet and have a serious talk with him and point out to him that not long ago there were passed, at the Hot Springs conference, a number of resolutions, which demanded, and practically agreed, that all those who were going to cooperate were to do everything in their power to increase agricultural production of all kinds. The report of this Hot Springs conference has been published and was distributed recently to the members of the House of Commons. It is called, " International Conference on Food and Agriculture." The minister would do well to pass a copy of that report to each member of the wool board, and ask them to give the matter more than ordinary consideration or at least a great deal more consideration than they gave the request from the wool growers of Alberta this year. I think perhaps that is as much as it is necessary to say just now. May I repeat that in my judgment the wool board has failed in its trust this year and is not entitled to be reemployed next year. As was indicated by the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe, $500,000 was spent in subsidizing Australian and New Zealand production and distribution.

speechtext: Well, my hon. friend frequently makes remarks like that in the house. People are producing in spite of the board.

I do not know about that,

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hon .gentleman should
know as well as I do. Then I find that this matter of prices was considered and thoroughly argued when the estimates of the Minister of Agriculture were before the committee. Apparently it is true that prices in the United States have always been higher than prices in Canada, but as I have said before we simply cannot tie our economy to that of the United States any more than we can tie it to that of Australia or New Zealand, where the prices of wool are very much lower than in Canada. For 1942-43 the average price of wool in Australia was 21 cents, when their currency was converted into Canadian funds. In New Zealand it was 22 cents and in Canada 25 [DOT] 9 cents. The percentage increase in Canada since the low prices of the thirties is 119-4, or more than double. In the United States, prices have gone up by 74-4 per cent, in New Zealand by 53-5 per cent and in Australia by 49-5 per cent.
But the price in the United States was pretty high before; I mentioned the figures.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes, but I think the hon.
gentleman would have to talk quite a long time before he could make a prima facie case against the wool board for injustice or failure of trust, when it is found that they have increased the price to the farmer in Canada by 119-4 per cent as against an increase of 74-4 per cent in the United States, 53-5 per cent in New Zealand and 49-5 per cent in Australia.
The price before the increase is important.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is a matter as to which there could be endless argument. All I can say is that at the moment the supply situation is very good indeed. We are able to get the wool. We do get it at a little lower cost by buying from Australia and New Zealand, even though we have to pay these very heavy charges for wnr risk insurance and freight rates. In addition to the price I have mentioned we are also paying a subsidy of four cents per pound, which brings the price up to 30 cents. Our price is such that, quoting my colleague the Minister of Agriculture, while the price in the United States for the same grade wool runs from 37 to 40 cents a pound, when we consider freight charges, duty and
everything else, the return to the Canadian farmer is slightly better than it would be if he sold his wool in the United States. The price to the farmer in Canada has more than doubled, while the price of woollen goods to the consumer has been kept down remarkably well when we consider the experience of the other war.

There appears to be some
misunderstanding about my statement in regard to the $500,000. I thought I made it clear that $500,000 had been spent under that item covering the administration of the wool board. I also mentioned that $130,000, which is the minister's figure, had been spent for the subsidization of imported wool.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is not right; $500,000 is the estimate of total requirements for the current year.
I cannot subscribe fully to the suggestion of the hon. member for Lethbridge that the wool board should be discontinued.
No, not discontinued- replaced.

Or even replaced at this time. However, I must say that I take the remarks of the hon. member much more seriously than the minister appears to take them. I followed his words closely, and I agree with a great deal of what he has said in regard to this issue. As he pointed out, very little consideration is given to the rancher so far as income tax is concerned. If a man invests his money in industrial stocks or gold stocks and there is a substantial increase in the value of those stocks, he can put that away as capital gain and pay no income tax on it. But if he has $5,000 worth of sheep held at ridiculously low prices, he is not even afforded a living wage when he looks after them. The minister has mentioned an increase of 119 per cent, but if a man makes an investment in a range, and finds that he has a gain, doubling his value, he must pay an income tax, as he turns those sheep into money. Therefore I say he does not receive the same privilege in that regard as is accorded to others. I find myself in agreement with the hon. member for Lethbridge when he says we should be fair to the sheep growers of Canada.
I believe the wool board should be urged to increase the price of wool. For many years in this as in other countries, sheep have been recognized as the golden hoof of agriculture. Yet in Canada to-day we have very few more sheep than we had in 1896 or 1898. It is true that we have a few more than we had in 1890, but between the nineties and this date there has been no substantial increase in the

War Appropriation-Finance-Wool Board
sheep population of Canada. Any increase there may have been has been effected in the hope of receiving a higher price for wool, in view of the development of the Canadian textile industry under the imperial preference of the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier.
In recent years we have been practically at a standstill so far as our sheep industry is concerned. It has been almost static; there has been scarcely any increase at all, with the exception of the last year or two. I must say in fairness that I have no fault to find with the wool board's administration. But I am in agreement with the hon. member for Lethbridge in what he has said about the general policy of the government with respect to agriculture. I believe it is necessary to have a wool board, because every other industry in Canada is regulated, controlled and strait-jacketed and. whether it is sound or unsound, it would not be fair to leave one out from under the cover of the strait-jacketing machinery. I do suggest however that careful consideration of the matters in hand should be given by these boards, and that more men with a knowledge of agricultural production, men who understand the different branches of agriculture, should be given places on them.
To compare prices received back in pre-war days with prices received to-day and say that they have increased by 119 per cent is not a fair statement. I do not know all there is to know about sheep production, but for many years I have kept sheep, and I know something about their cost of production. It is ridiculous to compare production costs in Canada with those in Australia, a country where the sheep may roam over land worth only a fraction of what a similar area would be wort-h in Canada. Then, in Australia housing is not required the year round.
It might help if the minister took the income tax off sheep and put it on dogs running at large.
Yes. Well, there have been a lot of hounds who have hurt the sheep industry. We have witnessed several setbacks, and most of them have developed because of government policies.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Sheep dogs.

Someone says they are sheep dogs. Often they are watch-dogs of the treasury. There is no class of live stock more indigenous to Canada than sheep. We have a cold country. We must build expensive farm buildings to house other types of live stock, in which sheep could be housed. They can be oroduced in this cold country

more economically than any other type of live stock. We have plenty of pasture land. There is no country in the world with such vast areas of pasture, and in such a cold climate, that has such few sheep.
All hon. members know that Canada needs foodstuffs. We have meatless Tuesdays and, if the war goes on much longer, we may have meatless Wednesdays, Thursdays and Fridays. We compare ourselves with Australia w'ith a sheep population of 40,000,000, while ours is only around 4,000,000, and for many years it was only about 3,500,000. That is our sheep population, in a country so vast. There must be some reason for this. I am not going to say what the price increase should be. We have been told for many years that we would have a great opportunity to sell our live stock if we had free trade with the United States. We have been told what a great outlet that would be. We find to-day however that in the United States farmers are receiving around 17 or 18 cents a pound for their beef, while in Canada we receive only 12 to 13 cents for the same quality. The hon. member for Lethbridge has pointed out that in the United States market they are receiving 14 cents a pound more for wool than is received in Canada-and this at a time when we need wool for our armed forces, and despite the fact that in Canada we have a cold climate and require woollen clothing. For half a century we have failed to increase the flocks of one of the most important branches of our live stock industry-sheep raising. We have failed to increase our sheep population for almost half a century.
I suggest the government should give careful consideration to increasing the ceiling price on wool. Other ceilings have been broken and have been increased. I am confident we will increase the production of wool in Canada much faster if we give the farmers some encouragement through an increased price than we would by following what I believe is going to be a most vicious policy if carried much further, namely that of handing out huge subsidies and bonuses. Some consideration should be given along these lines.
I notice that in this item the cost of administration has gone up from $200,000 to $500,000.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: We are dealing with wool at the present time, and the hon. member's observations are not in order.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Well, we are dealing with the wool board, for which there was an allotment of $200,000 last year and for which there is one of S500.000 this year. I suggest that perhaps the hon. member is in order.

War Appropriation-Finance-Wool Board

My objection is that there have been some changes in this wool board. For some time Mr. Dick of Cobourg was chairman of it, but changes have been made, and I should like to know why. Why did Mr. Dick retire? What is the representation on the board of practical men in the industry, men who are engaged in this very important branch of agriculture? I have watched the ups and downs of sheep raising in Ontario for years. Many attempts have been made to increase production in that province, and to follow the development of the textile industry there. I remember that some years ago the Hon. George Washington Ross, then premier of Ontario, referred to his dream-"Ye who have sheep on a thousand hills." Well, I go around through Ontario quite a bit, and I have failed to see any evidence of increased sheep production on those hills.
What is the set-up in connection with this $500,000 item? How many of the men on the board are practical men? The other day inquiry was made as to whether a report is submitted to each separate minister and what minister of the crown is responsible for these announcements and public utterances. I said that I did not expect him to know it all but the answer was that the wartime prices and trade board, of which this is a sub-board, was responsible and that public addresses, and I suppose reports and announcements, are not normally first submitted to the minister. 1 fail to see where there has been any effect in the way of increased, production on the sheep market in Toronto or Montreal, for instance. I notice from the Globe and Mail of this morning that prices are holding back and the market is very dull. The prices in Chicago yesterday were dull at $8.50. Buffalo is down to $8.50. Montreal was stationary and very little offering. The market was quite dull for live stock. The Toronto figures for sheep were:
13, 130 pounds, $10; 7, 130 pounds, $9; 4, 120, $8; 1, 250. $7.50; 3, 120, $7; 1, 120, $5.
There has been very little expansion in production. My last objection is that in the dying days of this parliament a report like this is brought down. Are we to carry on like we have in the last few days, like we did yesterday? Are we just a sounding board, are we to be a Charlie McCarthy for some outside ceiling control board that should be criticized far more than I am criticizing it this morning? We passed an item for another board all day yesterday and this morning they had the band playing outside the buildings, they were taking moving pictures and putting out propaganda to the public. This committee should have some control over expenditures of this kind; we are not getting the return we 72537-3021
should for the money expended, because the market remains very shaky, dull and unsteady. If this matter had been treated in the proper light by practical men in the industry production in Ontario would be far better.
They are talking about closing the house and we might just as well close to-night for all the control we have over these expenditures. We are simply sounding boards, we are simply Charley McCarthys for the ventriloquists on the treasury benches and their control system. Some of them do not know any more about it than I do, and I am not an expert on agriculture. However, I am just as much of a farmer, I know just as much about farming as some of the gentlemen sitting in front of the minister this morning. I doubt if they know anything about sheep, I doubt if they can quote the scriptures on it. The scriptures say, "Feed my sheep", and I think the minister is treating us as though we were a lot of sheep. We may as well go home because we have no control over the administration of affairs or over all these expenditures. We are sitting here to-day and to-morrow morning they will probably be taking moving pictures of the sheep in front of the parliament buildings. The hon. member for Davenport has not spoken for five days, I believe, and I have no doubt that when we pass this item his picture will be among those taken to-morrow, as are Charlie McCarthys to control.

As the hon. member for Broadview has now exhausted his second wind, perhaps we can proceed with the shearing of the sheep. I am in agreement w'ith the hon. member for Lethbridge and the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe. This question was discussed when the Minister of Agriculture was before us on at least two occasions, but we have not made much progress as far as dollars and cents for the producers are concerned. The percentages which have been quoted by the minister will not mislead the producers in any way. Two wrongs never yet have made a right. The fact that a certain percentage of an increase has been paid for wool does not justify anybody standing up in this house and saying that the producers are getting their cost of production. The argument made or attempted to be made the other night by the Minister of Agriculture was based entirely upon what the Canadian wool grower could get if he sold his wool in the United States. That does not convince any of us that we should have to go to the United States in order to find a basis for the cost of production in Canada. Surely there are statisticians here who can figure the cost of

War Appropriation-Finance-Wool Board
producing wool just as they can figure the cost of producing ships and planes and guns and bullets. I feel satisfied from the information I have received from wool growers in my constituency that the amount received last year, which varied from 25 to 26 cents per pound, plus the fact that the dominion government is paying half of the four cents subsidy on wool, does not satisfy the producers of this commodity. The figures given a few days ago by the Minister of Agriculture were to the effect that the price paid for wool this year, including the subsidy, would be 34 cents per pound. I hope that is correct. I should like to see the price increased to return the cost of production without the use of a subsidy. I do not say this because I am opposed to subsidies as such, but because I believe that if the producers of wool were given that to which they are entitled, there would be no need for a subsidy and there would be a better return in dollars and cents.

Has the minister the total amount of wool imported last year and what it cost the government in the way of subsidies and other payments? I should like to know also the amount of wool produced in Canada last year and what it cost the government for subsidies and other payments.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The only payment in the nature of a subsidy for which the Canadian wool board is responsible is the trading losses.

These amounted to $34,246.67 for the period from March 18, 1942, the date of the incorporation of the Canadian wool board, to March 31, 1943. That is largely losses in the handling of domestic wool. The four cents subsidy by the Department of Agriculture is an entirely different thing.
Mr. BLACIvMORE: There are one or two matters I should like to discuss a little further. The minister thought that probably I was speaking a little too harshly. I am going to read to him a letter from a wool growler in my constituency, and he will find that I was speaking for my constituency, which is one of the best wool growing constituencies in Canada. There was a meeting in Lethbridge last year. I heard that what went on at that meeting probably should have been a little different, and so I wrote this man for details of the meeting. He says in his letter to me of March 5:
At the meeting you refer to Dick, O'Brien and Brown were present. Mr. Longman, deputy minister, presented the ease very well for the sheep men and asked for a 10 cents raise, 35 cents against the present price average of about 24i cents. J. II. Walker-
He is the member for Warner constituency in the Alberta legislature:
J. H. Walker told how wages had practically doubled, shearing was 50 per cent up and lumber and posts were much higher, as was hay. We had to pay very high wages to put up feed this year. Help was scarce. The concentration camp at Lethbridge got most of our help. Ninety cents for jack carpenters and 50 cents an hour for common labourers. Two of my sheep herders left and went to work there.
This man Dick when he rose to speak told the wool growers to "shoot all they had as his hide was thick." He and O'Brien ignored everything that was said and continued to talk back. We got nowhere. They just came out west for a trip.
That is the impression which this gentleman made on men who were present at that meeting, and the men who were present were sober, solid substantial citizens of the Leth-brige federal riding. The writer goes on:
The sheep men at the meeting were mostly all large flock owners. The man across Canada with 15 or 20 ewes isn't much interested.
The minister will find that probably a good deal of his increase is coming from that source, from the small flocks:
Their costs are about the same but the range men feel the "pinch."
Jack Bowden, M.L.A., only received 22 cents for his wool as did many others present but all the satisfaction they got wrns that they shipped to the wrong grading house.
May I interrupt the reading of this letter to ask the minister, what kind of management of the wool situation in Canada he

War Appropriation-Finance-Wool Board
thinks this is when the individual wool producer does not know to what wool buyer to ship-his wool? Does that indicate orderly management of the whole affair? If there are different buyers throughout Canada who are buying wool and paying different prices, while we have a wool board in Canada which is supposed to be taking care of the whole matter of buying wool, that stands as a condemnation of the wool board or condemnation of the powers given to the board when constituted. The board seems to have plenty of power with respect to everything else; the marvel is that it could not take caTe of marketing. The writer of this letter continues:
Dick did promise to investigate the 50 odd licensed dealers. Many of the growers got a raw deal. Bowlen shipped to a dealer in Saskatoon.
The range men supply most of the foundation stock to farmers, small breeders, et cetera. Put the range men out of business and what is left of the "sheep industry" in the west would collapse. The small man is an "in and outer" in the prairie provinces. As a rule the man with one or more bands is taking an awful walloping right now because of high wages, scarcity of help, et cetera.
I hope the minister will grant that my remarks were no more heated than the spirit of that letter, and if he knew this man and how calm he ordinarily is and how fully experienced he is in raising sheep, I think the minister would be impressed too.
I wish to say a word or two more about this whole matter, because we are not finished with it yet. May I pause here to say that it is too bad to have to talk to the minister about these things, because I know what a lot he has to think about, and he should not have to be worried about matters pertaining to agriculture. But it so happens that the wool board appropriation is under his department; consequently he is in a measure responsible for it. The only thing I can do is to turn to the man who is responsible. One reason why we did not urge this matter further upon the Minister of Agriculture is that during the last three years he has reminded me of a horse tied up helpless to a post with children beating him. He has no choice but to take the blows, because somebody else is tying him up. I have pretty well grown weary of talking to the Minister of Agriculture, and I am talking now to the man who perhaps has authority to do something about this matter.
The Minister of Finance said something about agriculture being tied to Canada's economy. There is plenty of evidence of that. I do not think you will find in any other civilized country of the world the treatment that Canada is according to her farmers,
although the United States comes a close second, or did until a short time ago. The trouble is that the United States and Canada and a great many other nations have for a number of generations been scanting their farmers, shoving them and kicking them around, and then thinking the farmers ought to take it smiling and continue to do good work! The minister says that we are getting the produce, and I will grant that, but it is killing the farmer, and just as soon as they get a chance to move, the minister will have a hard time to keep them on the land.
In connection with this food and agriculture meeting at Hot Springs, I want to urge the minister to reconsider his attitude towards agriculture. May I show him what the results of Canada's method of dealing with her farmers have been. I have in my hand the latest copy of "U.F.C. Information," a booklet published in Saskatoon, Saskatchewan, for the month of June, 1943. At page 3 of that booklet there is a discussion of the debt question, which the minister still has ahead of him. This is the matter to which particularly I wish to direct his attention. It says:
It had been said that agriculture with about a third of the population of Canada had received only 17-8 per cent of the national income in 1926, 5 per cent in 1932 and 15 per cent in 1940-42.
If the minister thinks that is good enough, ma3r I respectfully tell him that he has quite a lot to learn yet. Professor Hope, of the university of Saskatchewan, takes these figures and considers them probably a little too dark and gloomy, and so he proceeds to apply four correctives to them. He finds this after he applies his four correctives to these figures, which in no way reflect credit upon Canada:
Taking these adjustments into account, it appeared that agriculture's share of the national income during the period 1926 to 1942 was at its highest point of 26'1 per cent in 1926. In 1929 it was 22 per cent, and thereafter it dropped to the low point of 13-1 per cent in 1932.
One thing which, among others, I was particularly anxious to impress upon the minister was that the agriculture industry, and particularly the wool industry, has gone through a terribly hard experience. Not sufficient allowance is being made for that. If Canada's economy is definitely arranged on the basis that the agricultural population of the dominion, large as it is, is to receive in normal times only 26-1 per cent of the national income of Canada, then Canada has to revise her ways a great deal before she is ready to qualify under the recommendations of the Hot Springs conference.

The hon. member for Lethbridge suggested before one o'clock that the wool administrator or the Canadian wool board, or both, had curtailed or limited the production of woollen goods in 1942 for the purpose of accumulating a large surplus of raw wool so that they might use that fact as a means of keeping down the price to the Canadian farmer. I indicated that I thought there was nothing in that contention. I believe the figures of production of woollen goods in Canada from 1935 on, up to and including 1943, furnish a conclusive answer to that statement. The yards of wool cloth produced in 1935 were 16,767,000; in 1936, 17,542,000; in 1937, 18,088,000; in 1938, 14,346,000; in 1939, 17,190,000; in 1940, 26,394,000; in 1941, 24,693,000; in 1942, 26,850,000; in 1943, estimated, 27,500,000. The figure of 26,850,000 shows the largest yardage since 1935. I have not the figures for the years prior to 1935, but that figure indicates what was the fact, namely, that the woollen mills were running to full capacity.
The object of the permit system which was instituted in 1942 was not in any way to curtail output. It was to allocate output as between military requirements and civilian requirements and as between what were regarded as more essential and less essential civilian requirements. The capacity of the country was fully utilized, and that being true, there was of course no curtailment of the production of woollen goods for the purpose of accumulating a stockpile of wool. A stockpile of wool has been accumulated for very good reasons. One has not known right along, and one is not yet sure, whether the supply lines between Australia and Canada will not be cut. If the Japanese got a little further south we would not get any more wool, and for that reason the Canadian wool board did the sensible thing. They aimed to get two years' supply of wool in Canada so that they would have the wool. They had a hard time getting wool in 1939, and since that time the situation has been kept well in hand. I think the Canadian wool board are entitled to the appreciative gratitude of the Canadian people for the way they handled it.

That is not exactly what I had in mind. I agree with the minister when he says that stability is the most important factor, from every point of view. Those who are engaged in business and who understand what this means will agree I am sure with the policy of the government and its advisers, namely that there shall be stability. But I have often wondered, and have interrogated several people who ought to know, why there should be this arbitrary ten per cent one way and eleven per cent the other. I have never gone to officials of the department, because I never felt free to do so, but I have wondered why these arbitrary percentages were established so early, and have been so rigidly adhered to. There must have been some basis for their establishment, but I do not think the reasons have ever been made public. I am not using the word "arbitrary" in any critical sense, nor am I offering any condemnation. But why the ten per cent and eleven per cent were so rigidly adhered to I cannot say. As a matter of fact the quotations show that the true rate has not always been stable. It has varied, as it did on previous occasions. But for the action of the Canadian government, in fixing it at an arbitrary rate, the rate at one time might be much higher and at another much lower. I agree that stability is all important. If the balance of trade were adverse, then of course we would have to pay for it in various ways. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Ten per cent was set because that was the market at the time. During the early days of the war the Canadian dollar went down in terms of United States dollars until the United States dollar was at about ten per cent premium. It was at that stage that the foreign exchange control board was set up. It was set up on September 15, 1939, shortly after the outbreak of the war, and it froze the exchange rate at ten per cent, which was just about the market rate at the time. The question is asked: Why is it adhered to? The answer is the same as the answer I gave to the question as to why has it not been changed, and why has it not been reduced. Stability is an extremely important thing, more important perhaps than anything else. If anyone can point out to me any national gain that would be made by reducing the spread, then the matter could be considered, but I think for every national gain there would be a national loss. I do not think the nation as a whole loses anything or is impoverished in any way by having these currencies in their present relation one to the other. While I am prepared to admit that a change would benefit certain industries, it would hurt other industries. The result of the whole thing would be dislocation and the necessity for readjustments. I do not want to talk about any particular industry, but it would be a blow to the newsprint industry to change this. If our friends in the west get to exporting quite a lot of grain to the United States, it would hurt them. The exporting industries would lose, at least at the outset, and the importing industries would gain. To the extent to which the government is an importer, the government would gain. To the extent to which interest is being paid, the persons paying the interest would gain. We do know that stability is a good thing for a nation, and when we try to balance the gains and losses against each other it is pretty hard to know what conclusion to come to.

It does seem to me that exchange should be based upon what a dollar will buy. maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I should like to say something with regard to the insurance principle. I endeavoured to say something on the subject when the estimates of the Department of National Defence were before us. The two departments are closely associated. The question, of course really comes under the department of pensions.
A person who volunteers for service must obey orders and serve where instructed, whether it be overseas or in Canada. With respect to the men serving overseas the present Pension Act may be considered fairly satisfactory, although there are some difficulties which are probably due to interpretation, more especially in the case of widowed mothers. But the Pension Act is anything but satisfactory so far as our men on active service in Canada are concerned.
Hon. IAN A. MACKENZIE (Minister of Pensions and National Health): I do not wish to interrupt my hon. friend, but there is another item for pensions. This item is for treatment.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Can we not have a general discussion on this item and then deal with the other items separately as we reach them?
The insurance principle in pensions originated during the last war. It wyas found necessary in order to prevent injustices which prevailed at that time. In 1919, when the Pension Act was first enacted, the insurance principle was included after due deliberation by the parliament of Canada. A few years after the last war, as a result I believe of the urgings of ex-service men's organizations, a commission was set up headed by the then Colonel Ralston, now the Minister of .National Defence. That commission sat for a couple of years and after a great deal of work recommended that the insurance principle should be restored and applied to all those who had served, and the Pension Act was amended accordingly.
At the outbreak of the present wTar the government pledged itself to apply all the benefits of the existing act including the insurance principle to those enlisting for active service. A special order in council was passed under the War Measures Act giving effect to this pledge. However, on May 21, 1940, the government changed its policy, repudiated its pledge, and definitely excluded from the benefit of the insurance principle all those whose service was in Canada only. True enough, provision has been made whereby a pension may be granted on compassionate grounds in cases of serious disability or death arising on service in Canada w'here those concerned are in necessitous circumstances. I do not think that that should be the law applying to all those who offered their services. But the fact remains that the benefits of the insurance principle have ever since May 21, 1941), been denied to those whose services in the present war have been in Canada only. Parliament later passed a bill which makes that the law. The pledge given by the government at the outset of this war should be lived up to. I think most people in this country believe in that principle. A soldier injured in Canada is discharged as soon as possible in order to get him off pay and allowances. He receives no pay or allowance while receiving hospital treatment, other than one dollar a month to purchase comforts.
There is also inadequacy of dependents' allowances and unfairness in the "means
4780	COMMONS
War Appropriation-Pensions and National Health
test" investigations under the present system. It is a downright shame that a widowed mother whose only son and support has volunteered for service overseas should have to submit to a means test in order to secure an additional amount of $5 a month over the $20 a month she is now allowed. She should not be put on a charity basis if her son was her only support before enlistment.
On June 18 an estimate was passed granting as of that date war widows' pensions. Provision was then made whereby a pension at the rate of $20 a month, might be awarded to war widows fifty-five years of age and in necessitous circumstances. While this is a step in the right direction, in my opinion these pensioners and the old age pensioners should receive at least one doliar a day or $30 per month.
I also think that provision should be made to give these widows free medical treatment on the same basis as treatment is now given to the recipients of the war veterans allowance. It will be realized that many of these widows are not able to earn other money to provide clothing for themselves and live on the present meagre allowance, and certainly they cannot pay medical and hospital expenses. Free treatment should be given them on the same basis on which it is given to recipients of the war veterans' allowance. If we cannot provide for these people and their dependents in these difficult times, I do not know how we are ever going to create this better world in the post-war period about which we hear so much and which people all over the world are studying, including a committee of this house. If we cannot set an example to men who have offered their all in defence of our way of life, it is difficult to see what the postwar period may bring forth.
I also think that there has not been proper coordination of medical man-power with respect to our civil and military needs. There is a serious handicap in many districts where the civilian population are not able to get proper medical attention. It would have a distinct bearing on the morale of those in the armed forces to-day if they were satisfied that their dependents were assured of proper medical attention when they need it. An effort should be made to establish greater cooperation between and coordination of medical services for the armed forces and the civilian population.
With respect, to rehabilitation, some improvement could be made. Under present conditions the clothing allowance is not

sufficient. With due respect to our price control board, everyone knows that you do not obtain the same value in purchasing clothing to-day as you received before the war.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Is my hon. friend referring to the clothing allowance on discharge?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: That is a matter for the Department of National Defence.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Well, much of the responsibility for rehabilitation falls upon the minister's department. As I said in the beginning, the two departments are so closely associated in these matters that it is sometimes difficult to separate them.
As I was saying, when a man is discharged nowadays he cannot purchase for the same money the type of clothes w7hich he was used to when he enlisted. Probably the same price prevails, but you do not get the same quality. That fact should be taken into consideration.
I am also of opinion that there should be some difference, based on length of service, in respect of the allowances granted when a man is discharged. He should be allowed at least one month's pay and allowances for each year of service that he has rendered. I served on a committee which drafted a measure dealing with compulsory reemployment after the war. There were ambiguities about the bill which did not satisfy me; obviously some of the problems involved cannot be easily overcome. For instance it is not always possible for an employer to reengage all his old employees when they come back. In this connection I suggest that every man who comes back, especially if he has served in a theatre of %var, should be granted a month's leave in order to visit his family, look around, and get his bearings. Then he should report back, and if there is not a suitable job for him, his pay and allowances should be continued until such time as he has received proper vocational training or is able to fill a proper job. Definite provision should be made in this respect.
In the matter of the welfare divisions which, I believe, are now operating through the country, great care should be taken to select suitable persons as chief officers of the various branches. They should be people with ex-service experience-I assume that in most cases, if not all, they are. They should have a human understanding of these difficult problems. When a man has seen active service overseas, particularly if he is a young

War Appropriation-Pensions and National Health
airman, it is difficult to get him properly rehabilitated. All these officers, therefore, should be endowed with humanitarian understanding of such cases.
In the matter of hospitalization, all hospitals should be located in quiet areas, to avoid undue disturbance of our nerve-shattered exservice men, and should be surrounded with proper grounds. Too often that is not the situation to-day. I am happy to say that in my native province we have a fine hospital in an admirable location. But that is not the case in many other sections of Canada. I am informed that generally speaking the surroundings are unsatisfactory. I believe that Christie Street hospital, Toronto, was originally a factory, and was taken over during the last war as temporary quarters. It is most unsuitable:	on one side are the railway tracks, and on the other the street cars; it is in the midst of a manufacturing centre where there is tremendous noise at almost all times, and all the surrounding conditions are anything but conducive to the welfare of the patients. I do not believe that many improvements have been made to that hospital since the last war-. I am informed that it is not properly staffed, that in some cases there are fifty to seventy-five men in a ward, that the ventilation is inadequate, the toilets and baths are practically the same as they were in 1918, and that there are many other defects. Such conditions as these are not good enough for those who have offered their all and as a result have become casualties. They are entitled to the best treatment and the most generous consideration possible. If we cannot provide fitting conditions for these casualties, it does not augur well for that post-war period of which we hope so much. I could spend a great deal of time discussing Christie Street hospital, but the hon. member for Hastings-Peterbor-ough, who himself was a war casualty and a patient in that hospital, knows something of the situation there and will speak on it. Also the hon. member for Parkdale, who is an eminent physician and surgeon and knows a great deal concerning this matter, will deal with it in greater detail.
I trust the minister will give some consideration to the points I have raised and those with which my colleagues will deal as we go along. The minister, being an ex-service man, is sympathetic. He may have his difficulties in these respects, but I trust he will take measures to alleviate conditions which are not satisfactory.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I wish to say a few words with regard to pensions of returned men of the present war. I agree
with the hon. member who has just taken his seat that in the present Minister of Pensions and National Health we have one who is sympathetic to the men and who gives prompt attention to any cases which are brought to his notice. Nevertheless I am afraid there are still some in his department, dealing with matters of pensions, of men now returning from overseas in the manner in which many such cases have been dealt with since the close of the last war, who have not the humanitarian views that he has.
I have two cases in particular which I wish to bring to the minister's attention and which, I think, bear out this contention. One is the case of a young man who was called up in Saskatchewan and who was suffering from stomach ulcers. He told the doctor of his condition when he was called; nevertheless he was ordered to report for military training, and did so. In the course of about three months because of the more violent exercises which he had in the army, and the change in his diet, he was hospitalized, remained in the hospital for a considerable period of time, and was discharged. When he returned home he again had to be hospitalized twice. The third time he was examined by his local doctor, who stated that his condition was so serious that he did not think an operation could be performed in the local hospital and recommended that he be taken to Winnipeg. His mother accompanied him there, and he was placed in a hospital and put under the care of a specialist who was recommended by his local doctor. His position was brought to the attention of the pension officers in Winnipeg, and they visited his mother in the hospital and asked that he be transferred to Deer Lodge hospital and placed under other medical attention. You can realize the position of that mother, with her son in a serious condition, in hospital in a city some five hundred miles from her own home, and having had a certain doctor recommended to her by her own physician. Naturally she wished to have the operation performed by the doctor who had been recommended; nevertheless these officials insisted that if she was to receive any assistance she would have to consent to the patient's removal to the other hospital. The result was that under this pressure she agreed. They said they would not accept the responsibility, so far as hospitalization and the operation were concerned. The operation was performed in Winnipeg General hospital. The minister's officials wrote to the department that the lady was quite satisfied with this arrangement, but immediately upon her return home she wrote me an entirely different letter. I cannot understand how she would say that she

War Appropriation-Pensions and National Health
was entirely satisfied on February 23, and on March 23, on reaching home, write to me stating that under the circumstances-I would not say she had been forced, but certainly pressure had been brought to bear which she could not resist-she had agreed, because she had already paid $40 as a deposit on hospitalization in the Winnipeg General hospital.

speechtext: May I have the name privately?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Yes. I do not think that is a fair way to treat men who have been discharged from our services. I have another case of the kind, though it is slightly different. A man returned from overseas where he had become a mental case. He was sent to Canada and placed in Ste. Anne de Bellevue hospital. His papers were lost, his people did not know where he had disappeared to, and the mother's share of his pay, which had been going to her regularly, ceased, and she received no further communications from her son. She wrote to me with regard to the matter and I took it up and found that this man was a mental case. I went to the hospital, and in conversation with the doctor in charge, as well as with the patient, I found that he was getting very fair attention, but the doctor stated that his case was such that, in his opinion, insulin treatment would have beneficial results. He informed me, however, that there were no facilities for giving such treatment at that hospital and that he would endeavour to have this man sent to Saskatchewan to one of the mental institutions there, where this treatment might be given. I pointed out to the doctor at the time that these institutions in Saskatchewan are filled to the doors, and that there is no room for patients there. It is a shame that our men returning in such a condition should not have the best treatment that science can give. It is something that should be taken up.

I am glad to hear that, because it is certainly necessary. With regard to this particular chap, I had a letter yesterday which I have sent on to the minister and I know it will receive his attention. As proof of what I am saying with regard to certain officials, this man's mother received a letter the other day stating that the hospital authorities were of the opinion that if the man were returned to his native village under familiar conditions he might be better off than he would be in the hospital where he was, but that she would have to sign a form

which would free the authorities from any responsibility, not only with regard to his conduct, but with regard to pension. If that is correct, it is a matter that should be looked into. speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Has my hon. friend sent me that case?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Yes, I did. I sent it either yesterday or this morning. With regard to widows' pensions, we have an act whereby the widows of men who served in the last war and who are receiving pensions, or receiving benefits under the war veterans' allowance provisions, will receive consideration. I think that this should be extended to all widows of veterans of the last war, not only bo those who are receiving pensions and those who are receiving war veterans' allowance, but to any who are in necessitous circumstances. We can well afford to take care of the widows of men who served in the last war, who find themselves in such circumstances to-day. They are all advanced in years, for the most part fifty-five or fifty-six, and the department might well consider granting a reasonable pension to all widows who are in necessitous circumstances to-day.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I wish to make a few remarks dealing with two subjects. First, I join in what the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross) has said in connection with the insurance principle as it relates to soldiers' pensions. He outlined briefly when and why the change was made, by which soldiers injured while on furlough in Canada would not be entitled to the benefit of pension. It is hard to understand why the department has adopted this arbitrary condition regarding pension to a soldier who is injured while on furlough in Canada, because if he were injured on furlough while serving beyond Canada he would receive the benefit of the pension act. To-day there must be many soldiers in Canada who were injured while on furlough. I know personally of a number of men in Christie Street hospital who have been injured while on leave; they have been in motor car accidents and some have lost a leg or an arm or other parts of the body. Some of them are in very bad condition. Not only are these unfortunate soldiers not eligible to receive the benefits of the act, but soon after their misfortune they are discharged from the army, thereby losing their pay and allow-

War Appropriation-Pensions and National Health
ances. It is quite true that the soldier continues to receive medical and hospital treatment as long as his injuries demand it, but in the meantime he is drawing no pay or allowances. It would seem to me only fair and reasonable that any soldier who has the misfortune to be injured while on leave, and who is not entitled to pension, should at least continue to receive pay and allowances until such time as he is discharged from the hospital. Take for instance the soldiers at Christie Street hospital who were injured in motor car accidents and who have since been discharged from the army. These men are drawing no pay and allowances. I understand that the only allowance they draw is $1.75 a month, which is granted them for hospital comforts. If that is wrong I hope the minister will correct me. When I heard of this condition, which seemed almost unbelievable, I took the trouble to consult an official of the department stationed at Christie Street, and he confirmed the fact that a soldier in hospital not eligible for pension, who had his pay and allowances cut off on being discharged from the army, would draw $1.75 a month.

I am very glad to hear that, because it seemed to me a most disgraceful condition that a soldier could be sent to hospital and given only $1.75 a month. A country which can raise billions of dollars a year for war purposes should be able to provide pensions for all soldiers who are injured while in the armed forces. I think the minister would be among the first to agree that any court of law would hold the department responsible to some extent for a soldier injured while on leave. Take the case of a soldier in Ottawa going on leave to Toronto, who is injured in a motor car accident. If that soldier had not been in the army he would not have been in the city of Ottawa; he would not have been on the highway between Ottawa and Toronto, and therefore he would not have been there at the time the accident occurred. Even though a soldier is on leave he is subject to recall at any time, and it seems to me a most decided hardship that a soldier who, through no fault of his own, is at a certain spot at a certain time and thereby is injured in an accident, as a result of which he is discharged from the army as soon as possible, is given only hospital and medical treatment, and he and his family receive no pension.
To illustrate what I mean, last Sunday in the small village in which I live a sergeant-major home on forty-eight hours' leave had the misfortune to be drowned. He left a widow and one child. As I understand the regulations, since that man was on leave or furlough his widow and child would not be entitled to any of the benefits of the Pension Act. I understand there are certain provisions under which a pension may be granted on compassionate grounds, or under section 11 (3) of the act, but that is only of a temporary nature. My understanding of that provision is that it is not permanent, that it is a pension granted only a short time and as a charitable gesture, while it is subject to review at any time. I suggest to the minister that this is not good enough. Take the case of this unfortunate soldier who was

War Appropriation-Pensions and National Health
drowned last Sunday. Surely his wife and child should not be placed in the position of having to accept charity. I submit that in this case the widow and child should receive all the benefits of the Pension Act. A moment ago the minister said the clothing allowance was not under his department. I do not know whether the rehabilitation grant is under his department or not.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Then I should like to tell the minister that the conditions which exist at the present time, under which an amount equal to a month's pay is granted, are entirely inadequate.
I should like to say a word about Christie Street hospital in Toronto. During the past few weeks various articles have appeared in the press, and no doubt most hon. members have received a document from the soldiers' organization, dealing with conditions at the Christie Street hospital. These articles in the press have been prompted by an announcement by the department that an addition is to 'be erected to this 'building in the near future. I should say to the committee that any remarks I make in regard to Christie Street hospital are not based on information contained in these various newspaper reports but are made as a result of my personl observations and visits to this hospital. I was a patient there for some time in 1919, and from that time until 1939 I visited the hospital on various occasions. Since November, 1942, I have been at the hospital twelve different times. To-day this hospital is in much the same condition as it was when I was a patient there in 1919. It is the same old factory building that was taken over by the government at the end of the last war, to meet a temporary emergency. Since that time it has been patched up in various ways; additions have been constructed, and so on, but the same overcrowding exists to-day that existed in 1919, except that it has 'been considerably intensified. It still has the same large, barren, poorhouse type of wards, with lovely old steel girders exposed, with wiring and plumbing running across the ceiling, and so on, for the sick patients to stare at day and night. There is no system of ventilation or air conditioning; perhaps those are luxuries which we cannot supply to our soldiers. Many of these wards have large glass windows facing south, east and west, and most of these windows are without awnings. I was at Christie Street hospital last week. Anyone who has been in

Toronto in hot weather will agree that there is no hotter place in Canada, but in that hospital I saw many boys in bed, seriously ill, with the sun streaming through these large glass windows without awnings, with only blinds to keep out the bright light.
I have been in various hospitals in England and Canada, but in my experience I have never seen a place so depressing, so drab and cheerless as the wards at Christie Street hospital. There is not a single bright spot of cheer in any ward. The beds are crammed tightly together in very large wards, and generally there is a second row of beds up and down the centre of the floor. Some wards have from sixty to eighty patients, and I doubt if such conditions would be permitted in many public wards in civilian hospitals since the time of Cromwell. Such things as easy chairs, chesterfields and so on just do not exist. In some of the wards the hardwood floors creak every time anyone walks across them, and the effect on a very sick patient of these floors creaking continually can be readily imagined. I know of boys in that hospital who have been seriously ill, boys who have undergone very serious operations and who, immediately after, have been placed in wards containing from four to six beds, while others have 'been placed in wards containing from thirty to fifty beds. I understand there is no such thing as a private nurse for any patient at Christie Street hospital, no matter how sick he -may be. The entire hospital is understaffed so far as doctors, nurses and orderlies are concerned, and it is only because of the great and tireless efforts put forth by the staff that the hospital has been able to carry on. But each doctor and each nurse has only one pair of hands, and any visitor to that hospital can soon see that with the hundreds of patients there, a great deal of care and nursing attention is required. The hospital is overcrowded in every way. As I said before, it is greatly understaffed. On my visit last week-end I saw a young boy who had a very serious operation on Friday of last week. He did not have a private nurse, because private nurses are not supplied. And on Saturday morning, while he was in a very highly-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I hesitate to interrupt the hon. member, but private nurses are supplied frequently at Christie Street hospital. The fact is that there were 613 vacant beds on June 30 of this year.
