War Appropriation-Pensions and National Health
he got out of his bed. Fortunately he was stopped by another patient before anything serious happened. I was glad to hear the minister say that there are private nurses at Christie Street hospital. Will he tell the committee how often soldiers are provided with private nursing accommodation at that hospital?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: At any time a particular condition requires it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Has the minister any record of the number of times each month private nurses are supplied to soldiers, and for how long?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I have not that information -with me, but I shall get it for the hon. member.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I should be interested in seeing it. The toilets and washrooms in the hospital on the third floor are simply a disgrace. On one floor, the third, with at least eighty to a hundred patients, there are four toilets and a bathtub. This is the same equipment that was there at the time of the last war. If there are any shower baths on the floor, I did not see them. The elevators look to be the same old freight elevators that were installed when the building was used as a factory. They are very large and clumsy and slow. In a case of fire these slow, clumsy elevators would be of little assistance in facilitating the removal of patients who are considered bad cases. The staircases, which are quite wide, are in the centre of the building. Probably that is not the best location for them, in the event of fire. Whether the building is fireproof or not, I cannot say, but I did observe that there are many things in the building which would burn.
The hospital . lacks recreation rooms, or rooms where soldiers may visit with their mothers, sisters or lady friends. The word "privacy" is unknown in this hospital. There are no grounds where the patients can rest outside, on days such as this one when the temperature is very high. There are no trees affording deep shade. The hospital is close to the tracks of the Canadian Pacific railway, where plenty of noise is provided both day and night. On days such as this, when most of the windows in the hospital are open, a cloud of soot and smoke comes through the windows every time trains pass. There are many- other factories in the district, all of which add to the quiet of the hospital by their steady noise, day and night. From the hospital window one can easily see the factory buildings of the Dominion Bridge company, which are located only a few blocks west of the hospital. This factory operates day and night and patients in the hospital can easily
hear the noise at all times. Street cars are only a short block away. In fact there is not one good feature or one good thing that can be said of the present location of the hospital. At its best it was only a temporary makeshift arrangement, taken over at the time of the last war. But through the years it has been patched up and added to, until to-day it is a patchwork with many additions and rambling buildings. If the addition now proposed is proceeded with, it will mean that Christie Street hospital will remain in its present location for many years to come, and that many boys who are now serving overseas will in the years ahead spend many dreary days and nights in this old ramshackle factory building. I suggest to the minister, who, I admit, has always taken a keen interest in soldier affairs, and has always given his most sympathetic attention to their grievances, that at this time, before the new addition is started, he should see that a survey is made to ascertain whether or not other locations can be found, either in Toronto or immediately adjacent thereto, where an entirely new hospital can be provided. It should have plenty of space, green grass, plenty of trees, running streams, sunlight, air free from dust and dirt and smoke of trains, and it should be a place free from noise and the eternal clatter which surrounds Christie Street hospital. I think the minister will agree that Canada must do better for her soldiers than to provide them with treatment in a place such as this hospital. In my opinion it is not good enough for the boys who are serving overseas.
At each session hon. members in all parties outline the very fine things they wish to do for the rehabilitation and reestablishment of the soldiers who return from overseas. Yet when we are dealing with disabled, crippled and wounded returned soldiers, instead of giving them the best in the country we are content to place them in a building which at best could be classed as no better than third or fourth grade accommodation. The various defence departments since the beginning of the war have built some first-class buildings and camps. Anyone who has been through the air force training centre at Trenton, or the Vimy barracks at Kingston, just outside the city of Kingston, or anyone who has seen pictures of the fine new naval building at Cornwallis, Nova Scotia, or has been through any of the fine training centres established from coast to coast, will realize that these buildings are most satisfactory in every respect. It is right that they should be. But they were all built for the purpose of training men for war. Surely if the defence department
4786	COMMONS
War Appropriation-Pensions and National Health
can spend so much money on buildings of this kind, it is not asking too much to ask the Department of Pensions and National Health to provide an entirely new hospital for men who will need it in the years to come.
Much has been said this session about the purchase of rugs, chesterfields and office chairs. Perhaps they were needed in the places in which they were located. But a few of those chesterfields distributed around Christie Street hospital would not be amiss. To-day at the hospital there are many boys who served at Dieppe. It is a disgrace to Canada to have to admit that the best possible accommodation that can be supplied to the heroes home from Dieppe is space in an old factory building like Christie Street hospital. One can easily imagine the feelings of any mother who goes to visit her son for the first time on his return from overseas after being wounded, and finds him in a place with the atmosphere of this hospital.
I appeal most sincerely to the minister to give his serious consideration to the question of the addition to Christie Street hospital. If the department insists upon going ahead with this addition, and insists that the hospital must remain in its present position, then I can only say to the minister that at some time in the future, public demand and clamour will be so great against Christie Street hospital and the conditions existing there that the government in power, no matter what the party may be, will be forced to build a new hospital in some other location.

speakeroldname: Mr. S. H. KNOWLES (Winnipeg North Centre):
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I shall confine my remarks at this time to one matter. I join with others who have referred to the subject with which I wish to deal, and I do so because of the minister's kindness yesterday in giving an interview to ladies who represent the people on behalf of whom I should like now to say a few words. I refer to the widows of veterans of the last war, for whom a special allowance was provided by this house on June 18. I understand that certain matters were brought to the attention of the minister yesterday, and no doubt he has had time to think them over. My hope is that he may be able to make some statement this afternoon with respect to three points which I should like to bring to his attention.
Before I do so, I should like to take a minute to offer a word of appreciation to the minister, or to the person responsible, for action taken on June 21. Hon. members will recall that on June 18, when we were discussing the appropriation of $400 000 for this purpose, I along with others had a great deal
(Mr. White.!
to say about the effective date of the payment. I was most insistent that it should be made retroactive to April 1. The minister sympathized with my point of view, but found it impossible that night to promise that my request would be met. However, when the order in council was passed on June 21 setting out the regulations under which these payments will be made, it included a provision for making the payments retroactive to April 1, although this was left to the discretion of the war veterans' allowance board. Like other hon. members I am still not satisfied with the amount, a mere $20 a month, but I am grateful for the action taken on June 21.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
On a point of order,
is the matter now being discussed by the hon. member in order? I want to say something On this myself, but I did not see anything in the list that would permit me to do so.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I think it has been the custom with all departments to permit a general discussion before the first item is specifically dealt with, and I understand that that is the practice we are following this afternoon.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I was particularly
anxious that the minister should answer these questions that I intend to put to him, because the ladies representing the women affected by this grant are in Ottawa at the present time, and it would mean a great deal to them if they could take the right word back to their organizations.
The first matter I should like to speak about is the administration of these allowances. It would mean a great deal to the administration if ladies representing what is known as the non-pensioned widows' associations could be given some say. I should like to see this representation just as effective as it possibly can be. I should like to see these women represented on whatever board is set up to administer these allowances. If there are technicalities which prevent the government from going that far, I trust that the minister will devise some means whereby ladies who represent the members of this organization, as well as those who are not members, may have some say in this matter. These women have been dealing with the problems of their fellow women for many years. They have at heart their interests, and, as I say, it would mean a great deal to the administration of the act if they had some effective representation. I believe it was the hon. member for Edmonton East (Mrs. Casselman) who emphasized on June 18 that the success of a venture such as this would depend largely upon the administration. I

War Appropriation-Pensions and National Health
hope that the minister, as a result of the thought he has given to this matter during the last few days, may be able to tell us that these women will be given representation in the administration of these special allowances.
The second matter about which I 'hope the minister may say something has been referred to already, I believe by the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross). It is the question of hospitalization for the women who will receive these special allowances. So far as I can discover no provision has been made as yet, unless the reference in the order in council of June 21 to the provisions of the War Veterans' Allowance Act covers this phase. If it does, I hope the minister will say so; if it does not, I hope he will give us some assurance that such provision will be made.
The third point about which I hope the minister will have something to say relates to the necessity, as I see it, of providing a larger sum of money out of which payments may be made to those who are to receive this special assistance. On June 18 the minister gave us a figure of between 1,800 and 1,900 women who were on the list of the department awaiting the passing of this grant.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: If I recollect aright, I said that the estimate made by the officials of the department of the number who would qualify immediately or almost immediately was 1,839.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: In any case the $100,000 which has been voted will provide $20 a month for only about 1,800 women.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: That is probably the basis of the estimate.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Hon. members will realize that in various parts of the country there are many women who are deserving of this consideration, and that their number must greatly exceed 1,800. I hope the minister can give us assurance that if the department finds that there are going to be more than 1,800 women who will qualify, a supplementary item will be brought down to cover the additional women.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
The first point raised by the hon. member was as to the possibility of giving definite authority to some of these women's organizations in the administration of these allowances. I do not think it would be feasible for the government to escape complete responsibility for the administration. I have told these ladies, and I think I have indicated also to my hon. friend, that we should
be very glad to avail ourselves of their services in an advisory capacity in the various districts. The procedure adopted is to refer these cases to what we call the local war veterans' committees, which I believe consist of the district administrator and two or three others. We should be most happy to have the cooperation of these women on these local committees, or to have them bring to our attention any cases of unfairness which should receive immediate attention. I do not think at the moment we can very well escape complete responsibility for the administration.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Will the minister try to see to it that these local committees to which he has referred get in touch with these women right at the start? The point I should like to emphasize is that it would be a much happier arrangement if these women were brought in at the start, rather than later on when certain grievances may have grown up.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I shall be glad to see that instructions are sent out to the local committees to extend the utmost cooperation to the various women's organizations.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Not only to extend it, but to solicit it.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: The second point raised by my hon. friend was in connection with hospitalization. The men who qualify for war veterans' allowances are entitled only to examination and not to treatment. I do not know of any country in the world that provides hospital treatment for the dependents of its soldiers. In reply to the third question as to the amount of the appropriation, steps will be taken if necessary to see that the amount is ample to meet the cases which come to our attention.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I am going to deal with only one phase of the work of the Department of Pensions and' National Health. It is with respect to a matter that has already been dealt with very effectively by the hon. member for Hastings-Peterborough (Mr. White). He has spoken of the situation that exists in the Christie Street hospital, from the point of view of a patient who spent several years there. I can only speak of it from the point of view of one who has frequently visited the hospital and has also been made aware of many complaints in regard to it over a period of many years.
To begin with, perhaps I had better refer to the number of petitions that have been sent in to the minister dealing with Christie Street hospital. One was sent by the Cana-
4788	COMMONS
War Appropriation-Pensions and National Health
dian Corps association. I shall not read the whole text, but I wish to refer to one or two items. They say among other things:
It is with the conclusion reached, that in war time adequate steps cannot be taken to effect a remedy, that we must take issue. [DOT] In war time, when the need is most urgent, many seeming impossibilities may be accomplished with good will and energy. Since nothing was done during more than twenty years of peace, there can be no assurance that, with the conclusion of hostilities, the present situation will be corrected. The outlook is made still more uncertain when the proposal to build a new wing of permanent construction is considered.
Many hon. members will have received through the mail a letter from Mr. P. B. Mellon, honorary national secretary of the National Council of Veteran Associations in Canada. I shall not read the document but will refer to one or two passages. This letter was directed to the Minister of Pensions and National Health, -and' it says in part:
At the meeting of the National Council of Veteran Associations in Canada, held to-day in Toronto with the following member organizations represented: The Canadian Corps Association, the Canadian Pensioners' Association of the Great War, the War Amputations of Canada, the Sir Arthur Pearson Association of War Blinded and the Army and Navy Veterans in Canada, I was directed to communicate to you the unanimously supported conclusions reached in respect to appropriate hospitalization of war casualties by the Department of Pensions and National Health.
His concluding words are these:
We are conscious of the duties and responsibilities devolving on us as citizens of Canada and as ex-soldiers. We cannot rest content and leave the wounded soldiers of to-day to the inadequate facilities and unfortunate surroundings of the present Christie street hospital. We believe you will understand and appreciate how strongly we feel in this matter and we earnestly hope that the evidences of your concern for the welfare of the men who have served as otherwise apparent will not be wanting in this instance.
I have put on the order paper a number of questions to which I should like now to refer. To one of them, regarding inspections, I have not yet received an answer.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: One appeared on the order paper to-day for the first time, so that naturally it could not have been answered by now.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Yes; the minister was not here the other day when I asked a question with respect to an inspection of this hospital, and whether regular inspections were made, and whether I might have a report of a recent inspection. I was particularly anxious to find out whether an inspection had been made with a view to determining the suitability of Christie Street hospital for the purposes for

which it is at present being used, and as to its suitability as a permanent site for a hospital, and further as a site upon which the government would be justified in spending over $500,000 for additional buildings. I asked if such a report had been made, and if so, that the minister lay it on the table. Is there such a report?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I shall be glad to answer that now. A weekly report is made on every hospital under our jurisdiction. Recently a special investigation was made by four medical officers, three representing the defence services and one from our own staff, who went fully into the whole question of the availability of sites in Toronto, and it was on their recommendation that it was decided to proceed with the extension that has been authorized. But there was no written report to me by this interdepartmental committee.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Thank you. From what the minister has just said I assume that the responsibility for going ahead with this construction rests upon the report of this committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: If I may interrupt again, I am not able to approve any hospital project except on the recommendation, first of all, of the wartime hospital committee.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Would not the final responsibility for what is done rest on the minister's own shoulders?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Oh, yes; undoubtedly.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Then the minister bears a terrible responsibility if he goes ahead with this project. A cursory examination of the Toronto city directory will show that there are from sixty to seventy factories immediately surrounding this hospital site. In the city of Toronto certain areas are set aside for certain purposes, and this particular area for a considerable distance around the hospital is set aside as a factory district. Any factory therefore may be built at any time in this district around the hospital. To erect further additions upon the already overcrowded grounds of this hospital site, as the minister proposes, is to disregard what is due to our soldiers who have returned wounded and maimed after defending us against the most cruel barbarism.
I should like to refer to some answers to questions that I received a few days ago. I asked:
What factories or industries are located outside the Christie Street hospital within a radius

War Appropriation-Pensions and National Health
of half a mile, (a) to the west of the hospital; (b) to the south of the hospital; (c) to the north of the hospital?
The answer to that question was:
Not on record within the department.
If what the minister has just told us is true, that an inspection has recently been made by certain officers who have reported favourably on the suitability of this site for an addition to the hospital, surely they have been derelict in their duty if they have not reported to the minister that this hospital is surrounded by factories.
Mr. MacNICOL; And coal yards.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Yes; not only factories but coal yards, and immediately adjoining, to the south, is a double-track railway, within seventy-five feet of the building, I am told, although the return says 115 feet. I shall come to that in a moment. Then I ask:
4. Do any of these factories operate continuously day and night?
The answer is, "yes".
The fifth question is: "If so, how many?" and the answer is, "No information". Will anyone argue that an inspection of this district is a proper inspection when that important information is not disclosed? Surely it would be the simplest thing in the world to find out whether any of these factories operate, at night. As a matter of fact the nearest factory on the west operates day and night.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Seven days a week.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Seven days a week, as I will mention in a moment.
6. Does any factory work at night with the help of donkey engines and searchlights?
The answer is:
The department has no knowledge of donkey engines or searchlights being used at any plant in the proximity of the hospital. An overhead crane, in use by a nearby plant, does not make enough noise to cause any interference, and the ueuropsychiatrist states that the sleep of the patients is not disturbed thereby.
The first part of that answer, in fact the whole of it, is contrary to the information which I have received. These searchlights are used in the proximity of the hospital; there is a crane which works at night, and a donkey engine which operates it, and the noise does cause such interference to the patients who sleep in the psychiatric wards that many of them are forced to go home and sleep in the afternoon-at least those who live in the city of Toronto and can do so-to get more sleep.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: The donkey engines the hon. member mentions are switch engines, I presume?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I suppose so-engines which operate the crane. These are in the McGregor McIntyre yard adjoining the hospital. I asked in question 7 if the neurological wards were on the west side of the hospital. The answer is, "yes". Question 8 is:
If so, what distance are those wards from the nearest factory or industry?
The answer is: "Over the fence." Just the other side of the fence! And yet we are told that these factories, operating in the way which I have described, can cause no interference with or disturbance of the patients in those wards. That answer to me, as a medical man, is incomprehensible.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: It is based on a report of two doctors who live there.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
All right; I get a very different story when I go home to Toronto.
9. Have any complaints been made of the patients in these neurological wards not being able to sleep at nights because of the noise from these factories or industries?
The answer is:
No complaints have been received by the department.
I asked if complaints have been received. They say, no. Well, that may be so, but if they have not received any, the department has not read the newspapers in Toronto, because letters from patients and friends have appeared on a number of occasions in the press of the city, complaining of this very thing.
11.	Are casualties from the present war placed in the wards with chronic invalids from the last war?
The answer is "yes."
12.	If so, does the Department of National Health consider this a satisfactory and proper arrangement?
The answer is:
The only satisfactory distribution of patients (and the practice in general hospitals) is on the basis of their illness or injury, with the proviso that casualties of the present war are housed by themselves whenever expedient.
Unfortunately it does not happen to be expedient to house them by themselves very often in the Christie Street hospital. I have had numerous complaints from friends of patients, young men returned wounded in this war, who were placed in a bed adjoining a chronic helpless invalid who has slept in that bed for the last twenty years. I wonder if that has not a depressing effect upon the
4790	COMMONS
War Appropriation-Pensions and National Health
young wounded man who has just returned. I leave it to medical men who are in the house if it would not also militate against the recovery of that patient.
The minister has already answered another question, having to do with the personnel of the wartime committee on hospitalization, which has had the responsibility of investigating this site and reporting upon it. These answers clearly show a pathetic ignorance of the real facts concerning Christie street as a site for a hospital-facts which could have been obtained in a few hours by a competent investigator. In view of the minister's insistence upon this site, I cannot believe that he has ever visited the hospital himself.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Oh, yes; several times.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Well, he is observant and
humane, and I do not understand, if he has visited it, why he would still insist upon continuing this monstrosity.
After what has been said so well by the hon. member for Hastings-Peterborough I can skip a good deal of what I had intended to say, because he has covered the ground. This building, as he has stated, was originally a factory. It was taken over during the last war and converted as an emergency measure for the purposes of temporarily housing casualties arriving at that time. The building is of mill construction, with the extra fire hazard which attaches to this type of building. It was never intended to be a permanent military hospital. The neurological wards, as I mentioned a moment ago, are on the west side next to the steel company's yards. Even the patients on the south side of the hospital are disturbed at night 'because of the noise of the trains passing a few feet below the building. There is very little space to enable the patients to get out and enjoy fresh air and sunshine, and if other buildings are put up adjoining the present ones they will still further curtail the grounds which are necessary and should be available for patients occupying beds in this hospital to enable them to get outdoors, particularly in the good weather of the summer and autumn.
Although the accommodation provided for veterans of the last war has been inadequate and unsatisfactory, I should like to say here that any criticism which I make does not apply to the medical or surgical staff of this hospital, which has been a most efficient one. I think we have at Christie Street hospital some of the best skilled surgical specialists to

be found anywhere, and they are doing extraordinarily good work under very difficult conditions.
I am at a loss to know why the minister seeks to perpetuate a situation which for a quarter of a century has been only an unsatisfactory makeshift. I do not agree with him when he says that it would not be possible under the conditions which pertain during the war to provide better care, for the patients for whom his department is responsible, than is available at Christie Street hospital. The erection of a new building on another site, where there would be ample grounds for recreation and fresh air in pleasing surroundings away from factories and trains, can proceed with great speed, as has been shown by the erection of other buildings during war time, and without the annoyance to patients w'hich building operations would cause patients in the already over-crowded Christie Street hospital if the building were gone on with there.
There will be no question of duplication of staffs until the new building is completed. It should be large enough to house all patients from Christie Street hospital who can be ultimately moved there, when it will be possible to have them there all under one administration in buildings of a permanent character with modern facilities and equipment if we are to give our wounded men who served us so well in this and the last war the very best accommodation that can possibly be provided. Nothing less than this will satisfy the people of this country. I do not believe that the argument which has been advanced, that materials and construction cannot be obtained for a military hospital, is a valid one. Recently the department of defence for the navy has announced its intention of building in Toronto a naval station of permanent construction. Surely such a building would not be given priority over a hospital to provide adequate care for our wounded men. What a hollow mockery it is to speak of a new and better world following this war if we fail at this moment to provide the most up-to-date accommodation for the care of those who risked their lives in their effort to save us!
I urge the minister, with all the force at my command, to alter his decision, even now at the eleventh hour, -in order to avoid inflicting additional suffering on our brave wounded men and forcing them to live indefinitely in a makeshift hospital with surroundings of which he and this nation should be ashamed.
To erect additions to the present hospital, where already ten additions have been made,

War Appropriation-Pensions and National Health
will encroach still farther on the limited grounds on this site; and what will you have at the end? Buildings cluttering up almost every foot of the ground, with no space for the patients to get out and enjoy the sunshine and fresh air, but daily compelled to endure the noise, smoke and dirt incidental to a through railway line passing close by and numerous factories.
If the minister insists, our people will be outraged and he will have committed an offence against the gallant boys who are returning wounded and sick after giving all they had in defence of our liberties. Surely they deserve a better fate than this. What right has the minister to deny these wounded boys the best possible hospital facilities in spacious, attractive surroundings with the maximum of sunshine and fresh air that will help to restore them to health again? Their relatives and friends, yes, the Canadian people generally, insist that this simple justice be done. Although the minister's term of office will come to an end in due time by the will of the people, this hospital upon which he proposes to spend over half a million dollars will unhappily remain to perpetuate the memory of the Mackenzie folly.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Taken over by the Tory government. If the hon. member wants to talk politics I will give him plenty of politics about how that thing was acquired.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I understand that the city of Toronto has offered two sites-

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: They did to the union government, but they were refused. They offered them High park in 1919, but were turned down.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I think they have offered them since then. I believe they would give sites now. I understand there are half a dozen sites in Toronto available, good sites, with plenty of ground in suitable surroundings and near enough to meet the criticism that medical men and specialists would not be able to go to a hospital situated at a great distance from the centre. I should remark that one of the visiting medical men at Christie Street hospital told me recently that he was unable to use his stethoscope when examining patients there on account of the noise and vibration made by passing trains.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: As a medical man, does the hon. member think that is possible?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I do not hear the hon. gentleman. I am going to make a proposal in regard to what might very well be done. It is to 72537-303
establish a convalescent hospital or home to house the very large number of patients now being taken care of at Christie Street hospital. I believe that eighty per cent of the patients there, who have been there since the last war, could be better looked after in a convalescent home where it would be very much less expensive to take care of them. In the first place, they would not require operating rooms or X-ray equipment or expensive laboratories, nor would they require the services of surgical specialists and physicians, nor would they require the same nursing care. It should be possible to procure such a place. I have not canvassed the situation in the city of Toronto, but I would suggest that one place that might be secured is Casa Loma, a very large building used at present for show purposes. I am informed that in one room in that building they can place a thousand soldiers at one time. I should think it might very well be used for some such purpose as I have indicated. If this were done, it would be possible to remove a great many of the old patients from Christie Street hospital and enable it to take care of new casualties arriving in this war until such time as the new hospital I mentioned could be built.
I have dealt with the question of convenience to doctors. It is claimed that first-class specialists could not spare the time to treat stricken soldiers who might be moved to a cleaner, quieter but less accessible site. I do not believe for a moment that the leading orthopaedic and other specialists would be so unpatriotic as to refuse to treat wounded soldiers if they are housed in a suitable building, even though it entailed a slightly longer drive in their motorcars. It is an unjustifiable reflection upon the members of my profession.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Would it not take longer for specialists to go, if it is farther away? And in that case they could not do as much work.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I think it is only a matter of a few minutes' difference, in any event. I should like to ask how this proposed treatment of our wounded men fits in with the declaration made by the Prime Minister two days ago when, speaking of our soldiers overseas, he said, "Canada will not fail them." Perhaps this is not the time to discuss whether the government has provided sufficient reinforcements, but this is the time and place to make good the Prime Minister's promise and see that a modern hospital is built immediately, with adequate facilities, on a suitable site with sufficient grounds to provide sunshine and fresh air in order that these patients

4792	COMMONS
War Appropriation-Pensions and National Health
may have every assistance in recovering their health. This much the Canadian public demands of our government, and nothing else will be tolerated.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I may change the subject a little, but before I make the proposition I have in mind, I should like to ask the minister if a burnt-out soldier now unfit for work receives a pension of $20 a month, irrespective of age.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Yes, provided that he served in a theatre of actual war as defined by the Pension Act, in dealing with the great war.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I should like to endorse what has been said by various hon. members with regard to widows of soldiers. There is no doubt that when our soldiers went overseas they took a great deal of risk, but the wives at home take considerable risks also. They are alone; they have to manage; they have sacrificed a great deal. If, in addition, they lose their husbands, I think they should receive every consideration at the hands of the minister. I should like to pay my respects to the officials of this department, from whom I have received nothing but courteous treatment. The only difficulty was that I did not always know the act thoroughly.
There is one matter I should like to bring before the minister; I am not sure whether this is the right time, though I know this is the right place and the right minister. In the city of Winnipeg an old friend of mine, Doctor J. R. Davidson, against whom I used to play soccer, has been conducting a clinic for the cure of cancer. In my hand I have a booklet which contains a reprint from the Canadian Medical Association Journal of 1941, and I am going to give this pamphlet to the minister so that he may become familiar with the work being done at this clinic. Doctor Davidson is doing a work that is touching upon the nation as a whole. Many cases which had been given up by a well known clinic in the country to the south have gone from Fort William to Winnipeg for treatment by Doctor Davidson, with very good results.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: May I ask where Doctor Davidson's clinic is located?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
It is in the city of Winnipeg. The hon. member for St. Boniface is acquainted with it and he may be able to endorse what I say. Let me give an example a little closer to us. The hon. member for Portage la Prairie went to this famous clinic in the country

to the south. There he underwent an operation and was sent home to await the last roll call. But hon. members saw him when he came into this chamber a short time ago, before he went back to Winnipeg for his last treatment by Doctor Davidson. He has been made almost new, and is very much encouraged. I am bringing this matter to the attention of the minister on this occasion because Doctor Davidson is not a young man any more; he is over sixty, at least, and I think the work he has done should be continued for the benefit of all Canada. I am sure the minister will see that this is done.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I am not going to deal with more than one subject at the moment. I should like to say something about Christie Street hospital, but there will be other estimates under which I can deal with that subject. I wish to thank the minister very kindly for his several references to my efforts, extending over quite a number of years now, on behalf of non-pensioned widows. It has been my pleasure to attend meetings of various non-pensioned war widows' associations in Toronto, Winnipeg, Edmonton, Calgary and elsewhere, and for many years I have been interested in their efforts to foster what I believe is the proper view in regard to this matter. During all that time I have found the minister most sympathetic. He deserves the praise not only of the women's organizations but of all who are helping these women to attain their objectives. He has been consistent in his support, though apparently until this session he was unable to do what he has told me on many occasions he wished to do, namely, to give consideration to non-pensioned widows. I am glad that this year he has been able to persuade his colleagues to 'let him introduce an item-I hope it is only an initial vote and that it may be increased later on-on behalf of non-pensioned widows. On the 18th of last month, when this matter was before the committee, I was unavoidably absent on an important mission in Toronto. I want to thank my leader for asking the minister on that occasion, even though the vote had been passed, to give me permission to touch upon the matter later. Perhaps I have no right to speak on it now, but I do so because the minister said he would permit me to speak at this time, and I thank him for that consideration.
On April 8, 1941, I appeared before a committee of this house to which had been referred various pension matters, including the question of non-pensioned widows. I was given a courteous hearing by that committee, and on that occasion I asked, first, that pensions should be

War Appropriation-Pensions and National Health
granted to widows of soldiers who during their lifetime had received less than 50 per cent pension. I believe at that time 50 per cent was the amount above which pensions were paid to non-pensioned widows and below which pensions were not paid. Secondly, I asked that pensions be granted to widows of soldiers who, during their lifetime, had received pensions of 50 per cent or over 50 per cent, but who apparently had recovered to such an extent that the pension had been discontinued. This would make the wives of such soldiers ineligible for pension at the death of their husbands.
In the third place, I felt that consideration should be given to non-pensioned widows of soldiers who had served in any theatre of war. I approved the vote passed the other night, so far as it goes. It is an advance over what we had. In the vote I find these words:
. . . compassionate allowances awarded by the Canadian pension commission to widows of persons who served in the naval, military or air forces of Canada during the war, 19.14-18, who are in necessitous circumstances, at such rates not exceeding, however, $240 per annum (or $300 per annum in certain exceptional circumstances to be prescribed by the governor in council).
And so on. During the debate which ensued this was further elaborated upon. The minister stated, as reported at page 3798, of Hansard, by way of explanation of the class of widows who are to benefit under this vote:
The widows eligible will be those whose husbands' service records can be thus described.
Earlier on that page they are described as follows:
(a) Widows of disability pensioners not now provided for and (b) widows of deceased recipients of war veterans' allowance.
On the next page something further is stated with respect to what is to be done under the vote. The minister states:
These conditions will be applied to the widow herself, but the age mentioned will be fifty-five instead of sixty.
I compliment the minister upon reducing the age limit from sixty to fifty-five. I am sure he would have been supported had he reduced it to fifty, because when a war-widow reaches the age of fifty years, in many cases, because of anxiety, she may not be in a very satisfactory state of health. However, a reduction to fifty-five years is something for which we may be grateful.
After interrogation by the hon. member for Vancouver South the minister gave a further statement, and outlined to the committee what I thought was some interesting 72537-3034
and worth-while information. The following discussion ensued between the hon. member for Vancouver South and the minister:
Mr. Green: The vote does not read that way; it reads as though the maximum a widow can get is $300.
Mr. Mackenzie (Vancouver Centre):	That is
income; but casual earnings are not classified as income. Casual earnings are in addition to the permissive income of $365.
Mr. Green: The widow, then, can get $490?
Mr. Mackenzie (Vancouver Centre):	That is
correct.
Mr. Green: Just the same as a veteran can?
Mr. Mackenzie (Vancouver Centre):	That is
correct.
That is a big step in the right direction.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
She has to earn the
difference.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Yes; the hon. member said that. She is permitted to earn up to $490. That can be increased later, of course, if the house so decides.
That is what the vote allows, but some provisions have been left out. The submission by the war veterans' association before the committee on April 8, 1941, asked that three classes receive pensions. I believe the first two classes have now been taken care of, but the third class, namely indigent widows of ex-service men who served in a theatre of actual war, have not been included.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: They have been covered.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I am glad to hear that. The minister has gone a long way in thus including widows of war veterans who served in any theatre of war. That is very satisfactory news, but I had not understood it from the remarks made the other day. However, it is something really worth while.
I know a number of returned soldiers who, perhaps on account of pride, and perhaps on account of a certain amount of stubbornness, have refused to accept war veterans' allowance. I do not find fault with them, because I like to see evidence of pride in any man. I like to see a man fight for what he believes is right. I have in mind one or two who have refused war veterans' allowance because they believe in their hearts-and I am not saying they do so either rightly or wrongly-that they are entitled to pension. Would the widow of that class of soldier be entitled to a pension, under the vote passed the other night?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
If he qualified for pension she would qualify for widows' allowance, provided he served in a theatre of actual war.
4794	COMMONS
War Appropriation-Pensions and National Health

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: The fact that he had refused it would not disqualify her, provided he was entitled to it.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
That is correct.
Mr. MacNI'COL: I am glad to hear that, too. I know of soldiers who served in the great war, who recovered from their disabilities acquired at that time, and who since that time have refused to apply for pension. They not having applied for pension, in the event of their deaths would their widows be entitled to the benefit of this vote?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Replying to the hon. member, I can give only my opinion. I am not sure, but I would venture the opinion that if one had been entitled to a pension at any time, his widow would qualify.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: They are entitled, but they have refused to apply.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I doubt if in that case the widow would qualify.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Then that is one class I would ask the minister to investigate.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Does my hon. friend refer to a man who had served in a theatre of actual war?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I refer to the soldier who has served in an actual theatre of war.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: The widow would be eligible in that case, certainly.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Then I think the minister has covered nearly everybody.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Yes, I think so.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I thought two or three classes had been left out, but I am glad1 to find they have not.
The amount of the pension was the subject of discussion at the last meeting. I have in mind what the Australians do. There the controlling factor is that a widow is granted a pension equal to the amount received by her husband during his lifetime.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I think that is correct, but I also believe they are reconsidering that in Australia.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I do not want to talk about something about which I know nothing. In the United States I believe they grant S30 a month to the widow of any soldier who in his lifetime received $10 a month. I had hoped that when this vote came up these

women would be allowed more than $240 a year. I hoped that it would be at least $365, or $1 a day. Now that the minister has gone so far this year, perhaps he will consider an increase by next year.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: The hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Bruce) is going to fire me.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I am speaking for Davenport riding which has many thousands of returned soldiers in it. I hope the minister will go farther and allow $1 a day, which would be $365 a year. The minister has rather taken the wind out of my sails by including nearly everything I thought was not to be included.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Carried.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
It will be carried in just a second if the hon. member will possess his soul in patience. I have been interested in this matter for a long time and I am glad that some results have been achieved. Perhaps at this juncture I should commend the non-pensioned widows and their associations for having worked so persistently over the years. They have come to Ottawa on many occasions at great expense to themselves, and if the minister has not done so already, I hope he will express to them the government's thanks for what they have done to help him and his department to bring about the results that have been achieved.
Someone else has said that these non-pensioned widows should have representation upon whatever board is set up to look after this matter. One or more of the prominent non-pensioned war widows in Canada might be appointed to serve on these boards or committees and to help to set up the machinery for the administration of these grants.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, considering that there is a treasury board operating in Ottawa I think it will be agreed that the Minister of Pensions and National Health has gone a long way toward meeting the demands of the exsoldier. I doubt if we could find a stauncher friend of the ex-soldier than the present Minister of Pensions and National Health.
I should like to speak about something that is a little local in character. Last year I referred to the general hospital situation and the lack of cooperation between other departments and the Department of Pensions and National Health. Since coming to Ottawa this year, I have carried on negotiations as quietly as possible in the hope of arriving at what I consider would be a satisfactory solution of the hospital situation on the southern

War Appropriation-Pensions and National Health
end of Vancouver island. I would continue to work in that manner, because I think it is the most effective in the end, but the end of the session is quite close and there would be no opportunity for me to express publicly my opinion and to ask for the minister's cooperation. I think I shall get it when I have explained the general hospital situation in Victoria.
We have two fairly large and efficient hospitals, one operated by the Catholic church and one as a general hospital. They are both located in fairly large grounds and are free from the type of disturbance referred to by the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Bruce) as affecting Christie Street hospital. At the beginning of the war the medical director of the army visited Victoria to look over the situation. We tried to persuade him to erect an addition to either one or both of these hospitals to take care of soldiers while in uniform or when they are returned from overseas, but we were not successful. Since that time a hospital has been erected in the naval barracks at Esquimalt. This was found insufficient to take care of the needs, and they have added to it. It is a good hospital with efficient equipment, but it is located in the heart of the barracks and is subject to the same noises that certain other hospitals are subjected to. Then they built a hospital at Work Point barracks for soldiers in uniform. However, this was not sufficient and they took over the normal school, which is located some distance out. The minister said the other day that it had cost $70,000 to convert this school into a hospital. It is a fine building, but it is not serving the purpose it was originally built to serve. It will cost another $75,000 or possibly 8100,000 to reconvert it to its previous use, and I hope that will be done.
In addition, a hospital was built at Gordon Head, which is about six miles from the centre of the city, to serve the officers' training camp. They are pretty well taken care of there. It is now proposed to build a hospital at Royal Roads which it is expected will cost in the neighbourhood of $500,000. This is the site of the naval college and is about nine miles from the centre of Victoria. There are no facilities to look after nurses or other attendants. They will not only have to build a hospital; they will have to provide transportation facilities, which are poor at the present time, and accommodation for nurses and other attendants. It is claimed that this will cost another 8500,000.
They could build a unit of equal size as an addition to the Royal Jubilee hospital, which is the general hospital. This is situated in a
twenty-acre piece of grounds. The hospital has sufficient facilities to furnish the required heating, as well as laboratory and other electrical equipment. This has been offered to the department, but they insist upon going on with their plans to build at Royal Roads.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Not this department.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
No; the department of naval affairs. I understand that this would not be acceptable to the Department of Pensions and National Health when completed, so that we would have at the very least three-quarters of a million dollars, and I would say . that one million dollars would be nearer the amount, spent on this hospital, which in my opinion would not be properly located for the boys when they return from overseas. It would mean that the patients would be at least nine miles from the city, and their friends and relatives who wanted to see them would have to travel that distance to do so. If conditions prevailing in the city of Victoria were anything like those that have been described as prevailing around the Christie Street hospital, or even the general hospital in Toronto, which I believe is pretty noisy, I would not object to going a certain distance out of the city to find a quiet and suitable place. But those conditions do not exist in Victoria. The buildings are modern and have every facility. They are both classed as Al. I am told that the cost per bed in the addition to the Royal Jubilee hospital would be at the maximum 81,250, while the cost per bed in the other hospital would be some $1,500 at least, and then the building would be of no value afterwards.
I think there has been a lack of cooperation between the three services in building their hospitals from the start of this war. I had hoped that that would be stopped by this time, but apparently they are still not ready to cooperate with the Department of Pensions and National Health and locate hospital additions where they can do the most good. I think the hospitals built in war time for the soldiers should integrate with the civic hospitals, so that they will be of benefit to the general public when the war is over. But that is not so in this case. I do not know whether the Minister of Pensions and National Health or his department has agreed with the other three departments on this proposal. If he has, I say to him now that as far as I am concerned I am going to oppose it, but I do not believe he has. If, however, he has taken a stand and is opposing the proposal of the other three departments to build this hospital, I will support him.
4796	'	COMMONS
War Appropriation-Pensions and National Health

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
So far as hospitalization is concerned, we are back where we were in 1918. We are just going to make the same fatal mistake in regard to hospitalization that we made in the last war. I was chairman of the hospital commission for the city of Toronto with Doctor Hastings and Mr. Thomas Bradshaw in the last war and for three years after. The city had been most generous to the government in giving it public buildings free in the last war because we were anxious to help, so that at the close of the war the troops would have proper hospitalization, adequate housing and proper treatment.
I should like to take five minutes to refer to the mistakes that were made as regards hospitalization at that time. In the last war we had a survey made of the hospitals in the city of Toronto. We had the old Base hospital on Gerrard street, located there when the Old Trinity and university of Toronto medical faculties were separate. Then the large, new Toronto General hospital was built, and these two faculties had been amalgamated for some years. The city joined with the Toronto General and the university in the new hospital. The result was a new General. The city paid about a million, the cost of the site near the great university of Toronto which has done so much for medicine. The result was a new hospital. I was on the board for seventeen years and on the executive committee with Sir Joseph Flavelle and the late Mr. Larkin. I was acting for the city of Toronto. The hospital was opened by Sir James Whitney about a month or two before the 1914 war. It was built then for to-morrow, and the city was generous and for years carried the deficits.
The war came and we found we had no proper hospital accommodation for the soldiers in the epidemic of 1917. I had a run-in with the government of that day, of which I was a great supporter. The late Doctor Hastings and myself and Mr. Thomas Bradshaw, who composed the hospital commission, were told that we were meddling in federal affairs. We were not. All we wanted was hospital accommodation for our soldiers and housing accommodation for themselves and their families when they returned from the war. I do not blame the Minister of Pensions and National Health altogether, except for not seeking new sites now. He is a Scotsman and I am an Irishman, and we do not often have so great a difference of opinion. I also appreciate what his doctors,

both past and present, have done, and his nurses and whole staff for years at small salaries.
During the flu epidemic in the last war I forced an investigation into the disgraceful hospital conditions for soldiers in the city of Toronto. I saw at Niagara camp, boys of sixteen, seventeen, eighteen and nineteen years of age down with pneumonia, and where were they? They were lying in camp at Fort George in tents, with only a bit of canvas underneath them to protect them from the ground. I talked to General Logie and to Ottawa about it. He was then the officer commanding that military district. It was not his fault at all. I asked him, "WTho is to blame for this lack of hospitals for soldiers?" The old Base hospital on Gerrard street had been closed up. It was not fit for civilians, and yet they wanted to open it up to accommodate soldiers. General Logie said in reply to my question at the inquest that a mysterious person at Ottawa was to blame. I asked who he was, but he could not tell me. I said to him, "If you had pneumonia, would you want to go and lie down at the back of your lot in a tent, with nothing underneath you but a canvas?" and he said "yes". I said, "No; you would go to the Toronto General hospital."
The result of lack of proper accommodation all over Canada for soldiers was that public opinion forced the government of the day to establish a hospital service across Canada at a cost of $35 millions, I believe, in connection with the municipalities, because when all is said and done in civilian hospital work, it is the municipalities that are putting up most of the money and paying a per diem allowance in support of the civilian hospitals, used by soldiers also. The per diem was fifty cents, but under Doctor Hastings it went as high as S1.75 to $2.25 for per diem patients.
The hospital situation now, even in all Canada, is a very serious one. I said that when the war started. I know that mistakes have been made; I have seen them. We have no modern plan of hospitalization. Some wanted to rebuild the old Base hospital on the old site, but we would not allow that, and it was torn down. What is true of civilian hospitals is more true of military hospitals. You can save a great deal of money by capital expenditure on the proper site and buildings, and later effect great economies in operation. We started out to look for new hospital sites after the above experience. I went out on the Lake Shore road with federal officials to look at a hospital site where the new Goodyear plant was about to be built. The roads were not as good then, and the

War Appropriation-Pensions and National Health
doctors, who were only part-time doctors, would not go out that far, so that we had to look for a new site. We went up to the district for which I have sat in three parliaments, in 1921, in 1925, and in 1926, and looked at the site of the present Christie Street hospital, the National Cash Register's new plant. It was opposed by the fire chief and other municipal officials who came out and looked at the site. The city at that time had absolute control over the property, residential districts and others, and hospitalization, and the law of the province did not allow them to ride rough-shod over the municipality in this connection, but Ottawa decided to get this National Cash Register place for a start, temporarily. It was opened about March 1, 1918, in the darkest hour of the war. There were votes for hospitals for soldiers all over Canada when parliament met for the next session, 1918-19. In every military district they were then at least waking up all over Canada to the requirements with regard to the returning troops. I opposed even then the use of this property. I did not think it was right to establish a hospital there. I supported the idea that a property be acquired, the old St. Andrews college, in the district of North Rosedale, near where I lived for eighteen years. The local residents did not want it, but I was glad it was secured. The quarters which were obtained on Christie street were to be occupied only temporarily. I remember the discussions of the subject at the meetings of the city council. I have a report of the medical officer of health, Doctor Hastings, who gave the government and the soldiers the most wonderful support, during and after the last war, of anyone I ever knew.
Well, what have you done? You have made ten changes in and additions to this property at a cost of $344,000. Great sums amounting to $444,000 all told, have been spent in converting the National Cash Register property, though neither the walls nor any other part of the building were suitable for a hospital. Other points were considered, including the exhibition grounds. In 1914 the new Toronto General was opened. If you had not had that hospital at the close of the last war, I do not know where some of the patients could have been taken for operations or special cases. Afterwards it was all done at Christie Street expanded. I say this while recognizing how splendid a staff Christie Street hospital had and has, and the grand work done there by all the staff and the civilian volunteer workers so long and cheerfully.
The present minister has done a lot of good work, and I am very much surprised at him as a Scotsman allowing the use of a building
like this as a convalescent home. I have been there several times. The building should never have been used as a hospital, and I am sorry we were not successful in defeating the various expansions which were approved by three parliaments, instead of new and other plants. I consulted the city officials on the matter, and I was very sorry that we ever allowed the key to be turned in the door for hospital purposes, but there was no option. I have seen the shell-shocked troops. I went last winter to visit a young patient whose father is a prominent citizen of the maritime provinces. Tor several years he was a member of this house and was on the committee which deals with war pensions and similar subjects. He sat as one of the more important supporters of the Liberal government. One of his children, a fine young soldier, was being treated there as a shell-shock case, and I was very much surprised at the condition of affairs in the ward, because the site was not fit for such cases.
The whole situation is, however, becoming intolerable, and a new plant is now required. I say that although I have nothing but admiration for the officials of the Department of Pensions and National Health, and for the doctors, nurses and committees that have dealt with this subject, because they know more than I do about it. But speaking as a layman who was on the hospital board for seventeen years and saw a great deal of the work done during epidemics of all kinds, when we had not quite enough hospital accommodation to look after the civilian population, I am much concerned at the condition of affairs and the industrial development which exists in the Christie street area to-day. The whole district is a' factory area. I remember the great separation of the Canadian Pacific from Yonge street right across to the junction in 'northwest Toronto. With the coming of the new right-of-way of this railway came factories, mills and other industrial plants. You ought to see the smoke and the dust and the dirt.
I am sorry to have to differ with the minister, but I am even more sorry at the mistake which has been made. Toronto has expanded its hospital accommodation at vast expense. The new Toronto East General hospital was opened and expanded, also Grace hospital, and in Toronto East it was intended that there should be a sufficient tract of land to provide a park. Then we have the splendid Western hospital on Bathurst street, which has been a big expansion. The university of Toronto is close to the new General property, and it is a revelation what has been done there in the
4798	COMMONS
War Appropriation-Pensions and National Health
past few years as a school of clinics for the university and the wonderful Sick Children's hospital of the Telegram.
I repeat that the site of Christie Street hospital is not and never has been suitable. The city authorities, I believe, are against this new expansion. All the business men I know of who have been connected with the various hospitals and have done so much for them are against it. I hope that the government will give the subject further consideration, because unless they get busy with more plants we shall have a serious situation after the war. I have talked to many officials of the city, and I believe that the city of Toronto or some private organizations would donate a site if the government would undertake to construct elsewhere a decent building. A plant with only 343 new beds will be of no good at all. To-day you cannot get into any hospital, public or private, in Toronto. You ought to see how crowded they are; some semi-private wards and public ones have twice' the number they were intended to accommodate.
I am ashamed at what I have seen at times in the way of accommodation at Christie Street hospital. You have a fine staff of doctors and nurses. If the obstacle is a question of money I would say to the minister, never mind the money. These men who went to the front and faced danger and death night and day should not have their welfare and restoration to health dependent upon a matter of money. You have spent 829,000,000 on a station in Montreal, a building devised for material ends only, which is being opened today, and yet you will not give proper accommodation to the troops who have served you so well in this war.
No municipality could get plans passed by the province for such an extension as this. I would not call it a convalescent home at all. I was at the Christmas dinner last year and saw the way it was crowded, away in a building at the rear in the smoke and noise and dirt.
Again I plead with the minister to reconsider his decision. You have to abandon that whole plant before long; you might just as well scrap the whole of it, the way we did with the old Toronto General hospital, and erect a good modern building. We cannot do without it. The new Toronto General has been built for to-morrow. The result is that it is recognized as one of the finest institutions of its kind on the continent. Although I should like to support the minister, I cannot do it this time. I feel very sorry when I see the parents, the wives and the little children of the patients going in there. It has not the proper accom-
modation, and Christie street is no place for a hospital. You will soon have to abandon it and supply up-tor-date accommodation. It is demanded by the progress of the science of preventive medicine, surgery and modern medicine; it will be demanded after the war with the numbers of shell-shocked air force and other casualties which will result from the war. I speak seriously, as one who has had a great deal of experience in this work. I have talked to eminent authorities and to members of the medical faculties of various universities, and they are astonished that we as a parliament sit here and take such action as this. It is a wrong step; it is a leap in the dark, and the money will be wasted-8500,000 thrown away on a place which should be scrapped as quickly as possible for a new site.
The minister has always been on friendly terms with the municipal authorities, and I believe that he could procure another site, which Toronto, I am sure, would provide, and the building now in use could be diverted to other necessary hospital purposes. I have suggested a location twelve miles out along the waterfront, or away up in the Don valley in North York, where the city has a lot of park land, near where the hon. member for Parkdale used to live in Bay view; it would make a fine site. If it is out a little farther, it would not make much difference because you have good roads. Toronto owns the street railway, the harbour property, the radials, the buses and a great many things. I know of no city which has given the last government and this government more splendid cooperation and support than all past and present city councils and public officials of Toronto. If there is urgency to have some immediate buildings, go ahead and build your temporary quarters for other hospital purposes, but provide a new site for these patients, for a convalescent home. I have seen some of the air force men who have come home, and some are suffering in a terrible way in this new war.
I did not wish to speak in this debate, but I felt it my duty to say to the minister that he is making a great mistake.
