I do not rise to take part in this debate, but I do want to ask a question of the minister on a matter of policy. In Canada we have the Department of Pensions and National Health establishing and maintaining hospitals at various centres throughout the country. Then we have the Department of National Defence erecting and maintaining a great many hospitals throughout the country, most of them of a temporary nature. We have the Department for Naval Services erecting and maintaining hospitals, and the Department for Air erecting and maintaining hospitals. Here we have four government departments doing hospital work, and so far as I have been able to observe there is no concerted plan of action between them. There must of necessity be a good deal of overlapping of services between them, and my question to the minister is this: What consideration has the government given to what is largely a duplication of services in connection with the three armed forces, and may I add the permanent service also, of which the minister is the head, and which I think is doing pretty good work. I am not going to flatter the minister, but I should like to say a good word for some of his officials. I wish 
to say this, that the department is so very different now from what it was twenty-one years ago that it is most refreshing. I recall that in the earlier days the pension department was in an evolutionary stage; the law on pensions had not become so stabilized as it is to-day, and the problems confronting the department were perhaps more difficult of solution than they are now.
What I want to know is, what consideration has been given by the government toward the question of hospitalization all over the country with a view-this is the thought that is in my mind-to saving a very large sum of money by removing the duplication and trebling and quadrupling, we might say, of hospitalization services? This problem of hospitalization is going to be with us for a long time. I have no doubt that eventually, when the war is over, one hospital after another will be closed up, and finally the department will take over all these hospitals. I recall that during the last war, when Christie Street hospital was set up, another hospital was set up at Ste. Annes. Nobody ever contemplated, I think, that it would be a permanent hospital going on for as long as it has, or a better type of building would have been put

War Appropriation-Pensions and National Health
up, and it would have been put in a different location. It is near the main line of two great railways and must of necessity be a noisy place. Whoever was responsible for setting up a hospital for mental cases within close proximity of two great lines of railway did not have much idea of the proper location for a hospital for people suffering from that ailment. I have often wondered at that; but there it is.
I think I have got my idea over to the minister sufficiently. What consideration has been given to the question, and what effect has been given to that consideration? To the onlooker, and I can qualify only as that, there does not seem to be any coordination at all of these hospitalization services. The Department of National Defence built a hospital in my city. The site was donated by well disposed people-I am not going any further than that -but the hospital is not now big enough for the number of troops in the locality. I understand that the ratio of hospital accommodation to the number of troops has to be over five per cent. They are building a new hospital in that city, and it is a structure of a most temporary nature. There is no foundation under it; it is built on posts but I assume it can be made warm by the usual methods of banking and that sort of thing, and it will be heated, of course, from one central heating plant. But it is essentially a temporary structure. I do not think the Department of National Defence would contend otherwise. The whole point is, why is there not a long view taken of this question of hospitalization? So far as the longterm cases are concerned, it seems to me they ought to be under one department.
Then there is this extraordinary situation. Every one of these hospitals has to have its own medical staff and its quota of nurses. The country is denuded of nurses because there are so many of them in these military hospitals. In one place at least that I know of these girls do not have enough to do to keep themselves warm at times; there are too many nurses there. I am speaking of the little hospital at Fredericton.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Not under this department.

I quite agree that it is under the national defence department. That hospital has seventy beds, ten nurses and twenty orderlies. It seems to me to be overstaffed. All the important surgical cases are taken to the Victoria public hospital.
I think I have elaborated sufficiently to let the minister know what is in my mind. I am not quarrelling with anybody or laying any charges of extravagance. But it seems to me
that each one of these defence departments wants to run its own show irrespective of the others, and I consider that there is a good deal of duplication, which means waste, too.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I think my hon. friend has contributed a pertinent and important suggestion to the debate. I would say that until two years ago what he has said was very largely true. The hon. member for Danforth sat on one of the committees which went carefully into the question of hospitalization in Canada and made certain recommendations. I myself remember writing a strong letter pointing out exactly what the hon. member for York-Sunbury has just now said. But it was largely inevitable with the development of new services. There was a lot of ambition there, and there was duplication in the early stages of the war. That is exactly why this interdepartmental committee on hospitalization was formed. That is their exact function. Their duty is to prevent duplication and, in consultation with our department, to develop a long-range policy so that we shall be able, when the war is over, to take over some of their buildings, of which they are to-day lending the staff to us in many cases, and thereby assisting this department which here and there is short of staff. So that I think, both in regard to personnel and in regard to property, there is now a pronounced improvement, and in my opinion it is a long-range policy, so much so that none of the ministers individually has the power now to develop a policy for his own department without the recommendation of this unifying and coordinating committee.
Which is all to the good.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I think it is all to the good.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: May I say that I have had a long day, and I should like hon. members to take note when I call them to order.

In the debate under this item we have had some discussion on Shaughnessy and a great deal on Christie Street, and Deer Lodge hospital, located at Winnipeg, has been mentioned. It so happens that Deer Lodge hospital is in the constituency which I have the honour to represent, and it is an institution in which I have always taken a great deal of interest.
As I heard the discussion to-night touching upon Christie Street hospital, an old factory with pipes sticking out all over in places where they should not be, having in general an appearance to the patient within that would tend to be depressing rather than helpful-that is, at any rate, according to what, was said here
4806	COMMONS
War Appropriation-Pensions and National Health
this afternoon and this evening-I could not help comparing it with the very much better institution which we are fortunate enough to have at the western edge of Winnipeg. I have watched the development there over a number of years. Recently there have been some improvements, and I have been greatly pleased to see the care which has been taken in an endeavour to make a hospital which would actually have a therapeutic value for the individuals who are in it. The surroundings are not such as I have heard described relative to Christie Street hospital, and the place itself seems to be in every way better. So that I would commence by commending the department for the general development which has gone on there.
Before saying anything further with reference to that hospital on a matter which is a controversial one, I wish to record agreement with the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Howden) in his remarks touching on a convalescent home. I believe that practically all countries agree that Canada has done an excellent job over the years in looking after its soldiers, and that Canadian pension laws are among the best, if not the best. But it really is very sad indeed to see the lot of some of these old veterans, discharged, as the hon. member for St. Boniface said, from Deer Lodge hospital or one of the other places, having the war veterans' allowance and no place to go, not thoroughly able to take care of themselves, and certainly not being able, with such a pittance, to have themselves taken care of. The department was always very good in granting domiciliary care to such persons during the difficult years before 1938, but I suppose that pressure upon the accommodation has sometimes prevented the department from doing everything which, might be done for such men. I urge most strongly that the minister as soon as possible deal with the erection of a place which may be described as a convalescent home, with some sort of secondary hospital accommodation.
The hon. member for St. Boniface also mentioned that in my city there is a dispute as to whether Deer Lodge hospital should be further developed, as the department desires, or whether a wing should be added to the civilian hospital, Winnipeg General hospital. I believe that both newspapers of the city, in a reasonable and well-reasoned manner, have supported the idea of not adding to this military _ hospital but of adding to the civic hospital, so that eventually that hospital will benefit. I believe the hon. member for St. Boniface is right in saying that in all probability popular opinion in the city of Winnipeg would favour that idea.
I know it is always easier to agree than to dispute, and for my part it certainly would be easier to agree, because so many of my friends have the view that the department is wrong and that Deer Lodge hospital, should not be extended, but rather that extension should be made to the civic hospital, so' that eventually the city would get the benefit. But members of parliament are not sent here as delegates. They must express their own views. Sometimes these will be truly representative of the district from which they come; sometimes, I suppose, they will not. At any rate, at whatever risk there may be, I must say that I think the decision of the department with regard to the building of the extension of this hospital in the way in which it is now being extended and the plans which are set down for it, is right and not wrong, and I think at this stage of development it would be wrong to try to build an extension to the Winnipeg General hospital instead of extending Deer Lodge.
Perhaps, if we could have had time at the commencement of the war to develop a policy whereby these military and pension department hospitals could have been fitted in with the general hospital scheme of the country, it would have been a good thing. At any rate that is the way it seems to me, looking at it in retrospect, and knowing it is very easy to be wise after the fact. But if we could only have foreseen the very great hospital development which would be necessary, probably we would have worked in our soldiers' hospitals with the civic hospitals throughout the country. But after we had a certain amount of development in the Department of Pensions and National Health, it was not feasible to place a section on the Winnipeg General hospital consisting of probably 200 beds and to send our men there from the army, the air force and the navy and probably some from the Department of Pensions and National Health itself.
In the first place I am reminded of this, that all of the returned men with whom I have ever spoken have objected strenuously to going into a civilian hospital. Now that is just their opinion, some person might say. Yes; it is just their opinion, it is true, but I do not know of anything that is more important in the hospitalization of troops than having the troops satisfied with the place to which they are sent, and I think the veterans, both of the last war and of this war, those men who are sick from time to time, in the army, the air force or the navy, and who have to be hospitalized, should have their opinion consulted and very great weight given to it.

War Appropriation-Pensions and National Health
That is the first reason why I think the department is right at the present time in extending the hospital rather than in building a wing to the civilian hospital. There are other reasons. If you put 200 men out of the forces in a civilian hospital you put them where their records are not, and I suggest that you have to have an administrative staff in the civilian hospital as soon as you put the patients there. If you put 200 beds in some civilian hospital and have the records of all the patients five, six or seven miles away, at the other hospital, immediately you run into all manner of problems and there will be a great deal of trouble.
I believe also that Deer Lodge having been already extended by the addition of one pavilion holding a considerable number of beds, 100 or 125, it was necessary already to put another clinical wing there, which was done, and one such step does call for another. If we could retrace our steps back to the beginning, we might make a decision in favour of establishing the military hospital as part of the civilian institution; but unfortunately after certain steps have been taken, I do not think that is any longer possible. Maybe we should have been wiser at the start, but I imagine that everyone will take his share of the blame for lack of foresight. I understand that the same problem exists in two or three other cities. Apparently it does in Victoria, and I have heard it mentioned as existing elsewhere.
Having said that much upon that one subject, I should like to direct the minister's attention to certain features of life at Deer Lodge hospital with respect to which it seems to me some correction is necessary. I know that in labour matters in the hospital the minister is not fully in control. That is to say, all matters of employment nowadays appear to be handled by one, two, three, four or five agencies. First of all, there is the minister himself; then the civil service commission; then the labour department through selective service, and finally on top of it all you have the treasury board, which gets damned here so frequently. In so far as this department can help the labour difficulties at Deer Lodge, I urge that this be done. Let me give an illustration of the sort of thing I mean. There are firemen in that hospital now doing much more work than originally they were engaged to do. There is no additional remuneration. They are firemen who are engaged, let us say, as the lowest grade type of firemen, and they find themselves pretty soon, as a result of the extension of the place, doing work that is usually called grade 3, or a higher grade of firemen. I use language in this manner only as illustrative of the problem. You have men
in that hospital doing the work not of one man, not the work that one man ought to do, but two men's work, and there is no hope of relief at all. That makes for dissatisfaction. It is not good for the hospital.
There are men whose circumstances are different. I am thinking of one man in particular who was persuaded to leave a certain job on the understanding that he would get such-and-such a position in this hospital. That is a couple of years ago and he has not got it yet. Where lies the trouble? I do not believe it lies right with this department.
I think that one of the superagencies has some way or another imposed a bar against this person getting what he should.
I mention these instances as illustrations of the type of thing I mean. I go to Deer Lodge hospital a great deal and I meet the people there. I suppose I know most of them by name. It is a large staff. If I do not know them all by name I know them to see them, and I must say I have found them throughout the years not a complaining class of people. But recently I have been hearing a good many such stories as the sort I have been speaking of to-night. I urge the minister to try to clear up all that kind of thing in this hospital. It may be the same somewhere else, in Christie Street, for example. I am sure the minister will agree with me that it is not the sort of thing in an institution that breeds and develops a good spirit, and if there is one place where a good spirit is needed it is in a hospital.
There are a number of other matters with reference to this hospital that could be touched upon, but I know there are many other problems besides this particular one, which is very dear to my own heart. I do not think I will extend my remarks further to discuss the other matters that might be brought forward, but I would urge upon the minister that special attention be given to these labour problems in Deer Lodge hospital, because it will redound to the credit of his department and result in better service being given to the men out of the forces already and those coming out of the forces, than whom certainly there are none who deserve better treatment.

I have before me order in council P.C. 1/5028 dated June 21, 1943. In this order in council, under the head "regulations", it is provided that the war veterans' allowance board may allow to the widow of a veteran compassionate allowance not exceeding $240 per annum except in such exceptional cases where the board may deem it proper to increase the amount to $300 "subject to the following conditions".
4S08	COMMONS
War Appropriation-Pensions and National Health
Then follow nine conditions which I do not propose to read. Section 2 of the regulations then reads:
For the purpose of these regulations "veteran" means veteran as described in subparagraphs (1) and (3) of paragraph (j) of section 2 of the War Veterans' Allowance Act.
I turn to the War Veterans' Allowance Act, which is chapter 48 of the statutes of Canada, 1930, as amended by chapter 48 of the statutes of 1936 and by chapter 16 of the statutes of 1938. Examining paragraph 2(j), subparagraphs (i) and (iii), I find that this compassionate allowance is limited to the widows of soldiers who served in the last great war, namely, the war of 1914-18.
I wish to ask the minister why that should be the case. In my opinion there is no principle upon which it can be confined to the widows of soldiers who served in that war. The widows of those who served in the Boer war should be entitled to similar treatment, for they must be even more in need of this compassionate allowance than the widows of soldiers who served in the last war, since they are older and, as a result, in most cases less able to provide for themselves. The definition of a veteran in the War Veterans' Allowance Act includes any former member of the Canadian contingent who served in South Africa during the South African war, and also any person domiciled in Canada immediately prior to the 11th day of October, 1899, who served in the forces of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and , Ireland in South Africa during the South African war. The widows of our Canadian soldiers who served in the Boer war should be treated just as the widows of soldiers who served in the great war are treated. I would ask the minister to give that matter consideration and see if something cannot be done to correct that situation.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
If I may deal with that point immediately, before my hon. friend proceeds further, I am very glad indeed that he brought up this matter. It may be recalled that the hon. member for Vancouver South asked me a question in this regard during a previous discussion, and I said it was certainly the intention to include the widows of veterans of the South African war. What happened was that the title of the vote was altered by an amendment, it being the intention at first to have it administered by the Canadian pension commission, and then at the request of the Canadian Legion this amendment was introduced. Inadvertently it dealt only with the veterans of the great war, but steps have
[Mr. Hazen.J
already been taken to have that situation corrected, and I trust it will be corrected by a supplementary estimate. Three classes were accidently omitted: widows of veterans of the South African war, the widows of imperial soldiers who were domiciled in Canada in 1914, and the children of such widows. My hon. friend will recall that under the War Veterans' Allowance Act widowers are entitled to twice the amount given to single people.
Is the widow with children to be so treated now?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Yes; that is the intention. These three classes were inadvertently left out when we changed the style and title of the vote in the house.
We told the minister that night they were not covered, but he would not believe us.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: My hon. friend did develop certain doubts about it, and after I retired from the chamber that night I became convinced1 that he was right.

I am very glad to hear the minister say that the situation is going to be corrected along those lines. That was practically all I rose to say, but while I am on my feet I should like to support the suggestion advanced this evening by the hon. member for St. Boniface, that veterans' homes be established to care for the men of our armed forces who, on being discharged from hospital, are not capable of earning a living on account of their physical condition or on account of their age, and who have no homes. As the hon. member said, when some of these men are notified that they must leave the hospital they say, "Where am I to go? How can I live on $20 a month?"

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: If I may interrupt my hon. friend again, the Department of National Defence is now developing institutions like convalescent homes for the duration of the war, and in all probability this department will take over those homes when the war is finished. I believe there is now one in every province.

That, I hope, will be
satisfactory.
There is one further matter I wish to deal with. I should like to support the statement made this afternoon by the hon. member for Souris that the insurance principle should be applied to members of our armed forces who have volunteered for overseas service but who have not left the shores of Canada or, in the case of navy and air force personnel, who may

War Appropriation-Pensions and National Health
have left our shores but are still stationed in Canada. The figures I am going to mention are not official, but I believe that at the conclusion of a similar period during the last war some two hundred thousand or more pensions had been granted, while up to the present time in this war I believe only some thirteen thousand pensions have been granted. Of course in many respects this war is different from the last one; the casualties have not been as high and they are not likely to be as high; but apart from it being the right thing to do, I think the government could easily afford to introduce the insurance principle in connection with members of our armed forces who have volunteered for overseas but who remain in Canada. Any man who volunteers for service overseas and who sustains injuries which result in disability, or whose health is affected while serving in Canada, should be entitled to a pension while incapacitated, provided his injury or illness was not caused by failure to obey orders or by his own misconduct. If death ensues as a result of such injury or illness, provision should be made for the dependents. It seems to me that this is the least this country can do.

Recently I received a letter from one of my constituents who told me that he was a veteran of the last war with an eighty per cent pension for gunshot wounds and nerve deafness. He sought relief in what is commonly called a hearing aid. He went to an electrical concern in Victoria, and for that hearing aid he was asked the sum of $189. I placed the matter before the officials of the department of pensions and was gratified to receive a reply in the next mail stating that this man had been communicated with and directed to report to Shaughnessy hospital to have his hearing tested and to receive an appliance. Then, as I understand it, the department is evolving an improved and extended system of testing for deafness and eventually hopes to establish stations at the principal centres, in order that proper tests may be conducted and hearing appliances provided. I am also informed that, aside from the Department of Pensions and National Health, people who are afflicted with disability in their hearing are endeavouring to form a dominion-wide association, to such end that there may be some comfort or relief from their disability. The understanding is that people who suffer from deafness, because of the discouragement and distress of being unable to know what is going on in their presence, commit suicide in numbers many times greater than do those who have the disability of not being able to see. The hope is that when such organization is perfected there may flow from it the good
results which have been achieved by the Canadian National Institute for the Blind, under the direction of Colonel Edward Baker.
May I return to a discussion of the price of this appliance, namely $189. Not long ago I was in touch with a civil servant, grade 2, who had been supplied with one of these appliances for $160. Then, I know of a man in this building who was approached within the past week, and who was asked $175. I am quite sure hon. members will realize just how eagerly a person so afflicted will reach out for any kind of relief. The people who sell this type of apparatus are high-pressure salesmen, and they put pressure on the government, just as they do on individuals. They will approach a man in a quiet room. These salesmen will have good, clear voices, and the experience is that when the appliance is tried out under those very favourable conditions the person who is interested can hear much better. But when he goes on the street with the same appliance, and is confounded with street noises, he gets no more satisfaction from the appliance than he would if an overhead or elevated railway were running above his head.
I appeal, first of all, not to the Minister of Pensions and National Health, but to the Minister of Labour. I ask him to have the combines branch look into this matter. It is generally conceded that these prices are maintained solely by reason of the patents controlled by the manufacturers. It is all very well for a person to pay a high price for a radio. That is a luxury, and it is one's own fault if he gets stung. Nothing could be so low, however, as the vulture who, as a manufacturer, takes advantage of his patents to prey upon the afflicted, and perhaps sell them something which in a short time will become useless. I am told that every part of the apparatus in more general use is made and patented as a non-standard or irregular size. Those parts are not turned out in standard sizes or types. The plugs, terminals, tubes, sockets, amplifiers and the cases in which the [DOT]batteries are placed are of such sizes that, if anything goes wrong, one must return to the company to obtain a replacement. It is impossible to make repairs otherwise.
I have gone into this matter extensively with people who understand what they are talking about. First of all, I am asking the Minister of Labour to put his combines branch to work on this matter. That may require some time. Accordingly I would go to the Minister of Finance, and request him to make inquiries of the wartime prices and trade board in order to determine just what a fair price for this
4810	COMMONS
War Appropriation-Pensions and National Health
instrument would be. I have been advised that I need go no further than to a man versed in electronics or to a good radio mechanic, either of whom could tell me the price for which such an instrument could be constructed. I may be wrong, but I place before the minister the information as I have obtained it.
I have said that one could obtain the information from a radio mechanic. May I point out, in passing, that at huge expense the government maintains a national research council. In their laboratories they have all the equipment for manufacturing signal outfits. To-day they are responsible for millions of dollars' worth of equipment of that kind. I am^ told that the signalling outfit is simply a hearing apparatus on a larger scale. Why not go to the national research council, put their engineers to work and find out at what price this apparatus can be supplied. Then let the government take hold of these patents, and pay the owners a royalty. If the patents belong to them they are entitled to some compensation. But they are not entitled to prey upon those who suffer. An affliction of that kind is bad enough; but on too many occasions a man spends his last cent of savings in the hope of getting just a little relief from the apparatus. I say the government is justified in asking the national research council to ascertain at what price this instrument can be produced. I have been told, on the very best authority, that the instrument which is in general use in Canada to-day can be sold at a profit for as little as $25-and that is very much different from $189. While it may1 be said I am talking at random, I am simply asking the proper authorities to have the research branch look into this matter, to ascertain just to what extent I am wrong.
There are other matters of a somewhat similar nature which require attention. I think, first, about artificial limbs. Anyone who suffers frofn the loss of a limb must feel the sting from the expense connected with the purchase of the relief which he must have. The government maintains such a plant, and manufactures these articles. Belts, limbs, hands, shoes and the like would be in the same category. My suggestion is that while the government has such an institution in Toronto, it might very well establish two or three across Canada. Let the government employ in such plants the men who have been conducting business independently. Pay those men good wages. They are experts in their line and are entitled to proper compensation. But I contend' it is the duty of the government to see that unfortunate people are not made to suffer.

The other day I came across a poor boy who is supporting a widowed mother. He has a small job but, on account of infantile paralysis it is necessary for him to wear a special shoe with a steel support, for which he must pay $28. It is true that this may have nothing to do with the department of pensions; but I.would suggest that inasmuch as this department has specialists who make these shoes, the government should be generous enough to let unfortunate people like this boy buy these at actual cost. To have to pay $28 makes a considerable dent in his little weekly cheque.
I realize that the minister's intentions in this direction are good, but I wish particularly to emphasize the importance of the government taking over these patents and providing the general public with such apparatus as may be necessary at a price which is fair and then paying an equitable royalty to the patentees.
Mr. MACKENZIE '(Vancouver Centre): I thank my hon. friend for his constructive suggestions. I think he largely answered himself the question which he asked in regard to hearing aids. The department has set up a board of experts who will approve all hearing devices. The intention is to issue and maintain hearing devices to those who suffer from this disability as a result of service. I think we have the newest devices and appliances available. We have also taken measures to control the prices at which these will be bought. They will be issued, without cost, to those who are pensioned for this disability.
As Minister of Pensions and National Health, does the minister not think this service should be extended to those unfortunates who are not ex-service men?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I doubt very much if we would have jurisdiction in regard to civilians. We are primarily concerned in this department with questions of pensions. We have certain fields of jurisdiction in connection with health, but I doubt if we would have any power to take such action at the present time.

I was sorry I was not here on June 18 when the question of grants to widows of ex-service men came up. It was found necessary to reduce the qualifications from eighty per cent disability to fifty per cent, but I think it might have been reduced to thirty per cent. These women are getting older, and I do not like the principle of making this appear like charity when it is their right. A short time ago the hon. member for Brantford City referred to Toronto General and Christie Street hospitals

War Appropriation-Pensions and National Health
and tried to compare them as far as noise in the immediate vicinity was concerned. They are not comparable. The Toronto General hospital is of fireproof, concrete construction. It is true that there is some noise from College street during the day when the windows are open, but you do not get that noise at night.
They go to bed early in Toronto.

Some of them do. Perhaps, when, the hon. gentleman comes to Toronto he has nothing to do and has to go to bed. I do not think the impression that these two places are comparable should be allowed to get abroad because they are not. Christie Street hospital was originally built as a factory; it is mill construction. One thing that has not been mentioned and that is very important is the number of trains that pass there. The hon. member said that when he was in Christie Street hospital he did not find it so bad, but conditions then were not like what they are to-day. There were not hundreds of trains passing at that time.

I
did not make any such statement.

I thought the hon. gentleman said that, but some one did. Conditions to-day are entirely different from what they were before. Think of the traffic there is passing along those lines and the traffic that will continue to pass until the end of the war. I venture to say that a large train passes there at least every half hour, and then there is shunting and other traffic. I should1 like the minister to tell me how many trains pass there per day or per hour. I want to know how thorough this survey was. I want to know whether he or any of those who made the survey ever visited the hospital and! spent a couple of days there to see what conditions were like. Did they spend a night there? There is a bridge factory quite close where riveting is going on all the time. I visit that hospital a great deal and I do not think the survey that was made was complete. It is true that we shall probably have to continue using Christie Street hospital because we are short of beds, but to spend $500,000 for, I believe, 340 beds-

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Over 400.

The hon. member for Brantford City said that this would have to be done as an emergency. Office space has been required in Ottawa and we have put up temporary buildings of one kind and another. The Department of National Defence built
a hospital at Camp Borden containing about a thousand beds. I do not think that cost any $500,000, even fully equipped, and it is a good hospital. If we have to have temporary hospitals, let us have them, but do not let us put up a permanent structure in a factory district where there are all kinds of noise all the time.
Can the minister state what locations have been offered by the city of Toronto? What is the construction of this hospital to be? Will he tell me anything further that he can in connection with the survey? I do not suppose this is the time to discuss the question of salaries paid to the staff, because that would come under non-war estimates.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
The building proposed will be of fireproof construction and will contain 460 beds. I have no information as to the number of trains that pass in a day. The experts who were there made a most thorough survey. They were men of the highest calibre, as will be seen by looking at their names which appear in the return tabled the other day. There were also members of the staff who live in the hospital and whose opinion should have some weight.
I have listened to the debate to-day, and with but one exception I cannot complain of the tone or tenor of the debate. I am largely in sympathy personally with many of the sentiments which have been expressed with reference to Christie Street hospital. If one listened to the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Bruce) one would think that I was the author of some enormity known as Christie Street hospital, whereas it was a legacy which I received1 from the government of which he was a strong supporter. I am far from advocating that this is an ideal location. On going through the order in council passed in 1918 I found that the city of Toronto actually offered a site in High Park as an alternative to Christie street, but that was rejected by those who were advising the government of the day.
The proposed extension is urgent; it is required immediately, it is imperative that it be built. At the present time, on account of the difficulty with regard to priorities it would be impossible to commence the building of a large hospital in a preferable place. That is the simple fact. In the second place, we could not have a duplication of staff at the present time because we could not get the trained personnel. As I said previously this evening, we are being assisted by national defence services who are supplying some staff to help with the more serious cases in our own hospitals. These are the two major
War Appropriation-Pensions

and National Health
reasons. I can see no possibility of commencing a major hospital at the present time. We have been in consultation with the authorities in the city of Toronto and have offered to send our officers to confer with the city authorities about a site and possibly to draw up plans so that they will be ready at the proper time. That, in my judgment, would be immediately after the war is concluded. The hospital could be constructed as a priority construction project on the site which the city of Toronto and the soldier organizations consider the most suitable. At the present time, however, no matter what my wishes may be, and I am as sympathetic as any hon. gentleman who has spoken in favour of better facilities, it is absolutely impossible to do anything but what we are doing in regard to this extension costing 8500,000.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The minister speaks of the drawing up of plans and the selection of a site for a new hospital to be built at the conclusion of hostilities. Has he any information to give to the committee as to how long it would take, after the conclusion of hostilities, to erect a hospital and put it into operation fully equipped to handle perhaps the large numbers of men who will have to be hospitalized during this war?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I think it would take at least two years to construct a hospital of the dimensions mentioned. I might say that there is other hospital accommodation in the vicinity of Toronto. The national defence department has a hospital at Oakville. We are to build an occupational centre on the lake shore, with about 400 beds. We have also recently purchased from the Oddfellows' association in Toronto a 200-bed hospital. So that there will be during the war many supplementary hospitals. Chorley Park is also being used as a hospital.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Does the minister not think the problem, which he is facing now and which he readily admits, and which I think has been pretty well established by the addresses made by hon. members who have taken a great interest in this problem, will become more acute than it is now as the war progresses?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I do not think so. With this extension and the supplementary facilities, I think we shall be able to meet any problem that arises. We have envisaged a certain reserve capacity in all our hospitals and I believe we can meet any situation that will develop.
As to the extension am I right in supposing that the proposal is to build stories on top of the present building?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: It is a new wing.
An entirely new wing. Is it to be a one-storey building alongside the large building there?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: It goes over the top of the kitchen.
Then it is proposed to build other stories on top of the existing foundation?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: That is right.
With regard to that foundation, am I right in supposing that when it was laid down it was built with the idea of carrying a great deal more than its present load?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Yes.

May I ask where these sites are that were offered by the city?
I understand that three were offered by the city.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Not one so far.

How much would it cost per bed to build a hospital that would be a temporary structure, not permanent like what is proposed to-day? I have another suggestion. There are many clubs around the city of Toronto which might be used for convalescent homes. I am sure that the citizens who belong to these clubs, golf clubs and so on, that are not too far out of the city, would be only too glad to let the department have the use of them. There was a great friend of mine in Christie Street hospital for about fifteen or twenty years only because he did not have any other place to go. It seems to me that with very little staff some of these clubs could accommodate a lot of beds. There is one hospital in Rosedale at the present time under the Department of National Defence, and the old government house in Toronto is also being used as a hospital. I cannot see the point in putting up a permanent building, in view of the length of time it would take to build a fireproof building on the present site and the difficulty of getting materials and labour.
I think it would take a very long time to build, and I suggest that temporary buildings be put up instead of a permanent structure.

War Appropriation-Pensions and National Health

The minister has been speaking of the difficulty of getting materials, of priorities and such matters. May I ask what progress is being made in the building of a soldiers' unit in the University hospital at Edmonton? I hope that is one hospital that will be satisfactory. The hospital is a wing of a civilian hospital there. It is in a district well chosen, quite easy to get at, and an easy place for relatives and friends to visit. It has been overcrowded. I saw the blueprints a short time ago, and I believe the money has been voted. When will it be completed? Might I make one suggestion. There is plenty of territory around there for convalescent homes. Convalescent homes of the cottage type might be built near the soldiers' wing in Edmonton.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: The specifications are about completed for the Edmonton extension, and the contract will be advertised in about a month from now.

A return that was brought down, sessional paper 327, shows that there are women in Christie Street hospital. Can the minister tell me how many there are there, and in this new addition will there be a separate wing set aside for women?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I understand that there are twenty women there, but most of them have been removed from Christie Street to Chorley Park.

Is
that the only place where women of the armed forces are treated?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: In every district they are receiving treatment.
There is no special hospital for them?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: No.

This item amounts to $4,225,000 and is described as being for "treatment and pension examinations-members and ex-members of the defence forces (present war)." This very item brings up, I think, the key problem with regard to the men who are discharged from the forces. For that reason I am sorry that the minister has not seen fit to explain the stand of the government with regard to a suggestion that has been made by many of the members of the house to-day that the insurance principle should be reinstated in dealing with pension applications from men who have not served beyond Canada. So
many men have been discharged from the forces during the present war as medically unfit. I think every member of the house has found it difficult to understand why such a large number of men taken in as category A should become unfit during their service in the forces. Yet that is the case. Thousands and thousands of men have been taken in as category A and discharged as category E, but only a very small proportion of them have been able to qualify for pension. I am not blaming that particularly on the minister's department; I think perhaps it was because of the law; and I suggest that the law should be altered. As the minister knows, throughout the whole of the last war the men in the forces were protected by this insurance principle. That principle is to be found in section 11, subsection 1, paragraph (a) of the Pension Act, which states in effect that a man can get a pension, where the injury or disease or aggravation thereof-and "aggravation thereof" is important with regard to disease, particularly-was attributable to or was incurred -these are the key words, "or was incurred"- during such military service. In other words, in. the last war, if men were taken in as fit, and they became unfit on account of injury or disease, whether they served in Canada or overseas, they were entitled to a pension. The same principle applied during the present war up to and including May 20, 1940. At the outbreak of war the government by order in council made that principle applicable. But then, for some reason or another, a change was made, and now the insurance principle applies only where a man has served out of Canada; if he has served within Canada only he must show that his injury or his disease or the aggravation thereof arose out of or was directly connected with military service. I know in my own experience, particularly in the case of disease, time after time the man cannot qualify for a pension. He enlists category A; he comes out category E, perhaps disabled for life, but he cannot qualify for a pension. One cannot explain that to the public, nor can one explain it to the man. People take the view, "This man was perfectly fit when he enlisted; he has been in the army and has come out unfit; he should get some pension." I suggest to hon. members that this provision must be changed, and changed without any further delay.
We had an argument about that in the committee on returned soldier problems which sat in 1941, I think it was. As a result a compromise was reached and subsection 3 of
4814	COMMONS
War Appropriation-Pensions and National Health
section 11 of the Pension Act was inserted. That deals only with hardship cases, where a man is in necessitous circumstances and where his disability is serious; in the discretion of the commission he may be awarded some pension; the commission also has discretion as to the amount. Some cases have been covered under that section, so that it was of benefit. But I suggest that the time has now come to go the whole length and restore the insurance principle to the pension law of Canada. I suggest to the minister that where a man enlists, is qualified to go overseas, and is ready to go overseas, or in other words is regarded by the public as ready to go and do the fighting, that man should be covered by the insurance principle. I do not ask it for the men who are going to stay in Canada, but on behalf of the men who enlist to go and fight.
I do not wrnnt to weary hon. members, but there was a return brought down on April 1, 1943, order No. 98, in answer to a question by the hon. member for Lake Centre. It shows that, as of December 31 last year, 64,401 men had been discharged from the three forces as medically unfit. Of that number, 57,118 were men who had served only in Canada. The same return shows that, as of January 31, 1943, just a month later than the army figures, there had been only 3,286 pensions granted and another 1,500 had been allowed but were not actually in payment, making a total of 4,786.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: It is 7,000 now.
Well, there have been more men discharged since those dates.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Oh, yes.
And of course more pensions have been granted. But the proportion is very, very small. My submission is that that shows there is something wrong with our pension law as it stands at the present time.
All the 64,000 must have been A category when they went in.
I asked a question back in March to get that information. An order was passed on March 29, but I have not yet got the answer.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
Does my hon. friend say that an order affecting our department was passed in March?
TMr. Green.]

On March 29 an order was passed for an answer to these questions by myself:
.1. How many men who w'ere taken on the strength of the Canadian army as being in category "A" have been discharged as category "E"?
2.	Of this number, how many became category "E" during service abroad?
In other words, they would be covered by the insurance principle.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: That is another department.

The next question:
3.	How many of the last-mentioned group have been granted pensions?
4.	Howr many have been granted pensions who became category "E" during service in Canada?
I have not yet been able to get an answer to those questions.
This defect in the pension law has a further result. The man who is discharged as medically unfit is handicapped in getting treatment. If he gets a pension he is entitled to treatment, but in other cases he can get treatment, I believe, only for a period of a year. I believe he can now get free treatment for a year?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
Yes.
Mr, GREEN: Every discharged man can. But in some cases a man cannot be cured in a year. I have on my desk now the papers in the case of a man who has had to take expensive treatments running for more than a year, and he is unable-

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: He can get treatment to the completion of the treatment.
This man has been unable to get it. The treatments were stopped at the end of the year. I took the matter up with the department.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Could I have the details of that case?

I will give the minister the case. If these men had been granted pensions they would get the treatment.
Finally, one other point which I wish the minister would clear up is with regard to the programme for reconditioning men. We were told about a year ago last Easter that there was some great plan on foot for reconditioning men. If a man had hernia or some other trouble which could be cured, he was to be taken in to a departmental hospital and treated so that he would become fit. We have never

War Appropriation-Pensions and National Health
been able to find out just what was done along that line. I wish the minister would tell us now how far the government has got with this reconditioning programme, both for men who were about to enlist and for men who were already in the forces.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: In regard to reconditioning cases, of course that is no longer proceeding under this department. There is a subsequent order in council to which I referred the other day, whereunder they are taken in in lower categories, and this work is being carried out under national defence department auspices. That is under order in council 2291 and order in council 2229. Up to January 1, 1943, there were 689 cases altogether.
How many was it expected would be treated' under that provision? We thought there were going to be a good many thousands.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I have no estimate now.
Has the plan broken down, or is it being carried on actively?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: It has been taken over by another department and the reconditioning is done direct by national defence.

What about this Pension
Act and the insurance principle?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: That is an old question of discussion between my hon. friend and myself.
I think the minister would agree with me if he could speak sub rosa, or under the table.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
I will not contradict my hon. friend on that point at all. My hon. friend knows that we discussed it thoroughly, as he mentioned, in 1941. Without a question of doubt a substantial body of opinion in the country favours the adoption of the insurance principle, and among ex-servicemen themselves, I believe, opinion is more or less unanimous, as indicated at various conventions of ex-servicemen.
I think the broadening we were able to effect-in 1941 did a tremendous amount of good. About ten per cent of the cases were allowed under section 11, subsection 3. Of the 7,000, roughly 719 were allowed, which has proved to be beneficial in difficult cases. My hon. friend is aware that we did extend1 substantially the definition of theatre of active war, so that the only people excluded to-day from the
insurance principle are those who never left Canada. Those who go overseas and come back are protected for the rest of their service in Canada until the conclusion of the war, and in regard to the air force, the navy and the army, they are all protected outside Canada and in certain cases, as referred to by my hon. friend, within Canada, although those cases are not likely to arise.
Whether the insurance principle should be adopted or not is a question of government policy on which I am not free to say more than I have said, but I am fully aware of the demand for it, especially on the part of exservicemen, and my sympathies might be strongly in favour of it if I were free to express them.	.

I wish to add a word to the discussion that has taken place between the member for Vancouver South and the Minister of Pensions. Speaking as a returned man, I am pleased to hear the hon. member for Vancouver South echo my own thought, that the returned men generally could hardly hope to have a more sympathetic minister handling the affairs of this department than the present Minister of Pensions and National Health. We are all agreed that he is moved by a great desire to be not only fair but very generous, and that is as it should be in our attitude to the men who enlist for active service.
I suggest to the minister that in this particular war the ability to determine health conditions and the true category of enlisted men is much greater than it was in the last war. I can see that in the last war, owing to the difficulty which the medical officers had in examining men on enlistment, there would be some cases that would be open to doubt whether the injury or illness had resulted from service conditions. But in this particular war, it seems to me, we have so improved the X-ray examinations and other methods now known to medical science as to exclude the possibility of certain physical weaknesses not being detected, and we have taken such great care in the application of these new safeguards against men getting into the armed services who are not physically fit that I, like the hon. member for Vancouver South, feel that the time has come definitely when this country should embark upon the insurance principle which he has discussed so ably. As a returned man and a member of the Liberal party, I join with him in urging the minister to continue the struggle to have that principle adopted, knowing how difficult it is for the individual to discharge the onus of substantiating his case before any tribunal if the facts are difficult to ascertain. On the other hand, the department has the
4816	COMMONS
War Appropriation-Pensions and National Health
records and all the ability to determine at the time of enlistment a man's physical condition, and having given him a category and accepted his services, we should assume the responsibility that goes with that acceptance and see that the principle is adopted as a basic principle in the Canadian treatment of soldiers, sailors and airmen on active service.

I would be heartily in favour of what has been advocated by the two previous speakers but for the doubts and misgivings I have arising out of the high proportion numerically of those who have been mustered out of the army, the navy and the air force within a comparatively short time after their enlistment. Those figures would surely give a layman an impression contrary to that suggested by the hon. member for Swift Current.

I believe there is a provisional period that still permits of further examination, and some of those figures will refer to those persons who are further examined and found not to be in a proper state of health.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: That is of recent origin, I am told by my advisers. In regard to those discharged, it is only fair to point out that up to March 31, 1943, 19-5 per cent in the army had less than three months' service, 42-9 per cent had less than six months and 69-4 per cent had less than one year's service.
And over one year?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: It is 30-6 per cent.

On the basis of those
figures it does seem to me that if you are to adopt the insurance principle, using that term in its best sense, there would need to be considerable tightening up in the medical examination of the men at the time they are inducted into the Canadian army. The tact that there is such a high proportion suggests to my mind at least that the medical examination of these men at the time they were inducted into the service was not of the kind to which the hon. member for Swift Current has referred; otherwise surely there would not be those numbers or that proportion of men discharged from the army in category E within such comparatively short periods. It seems to me inconceivable that a proper medical examination would not have disclosed a much higher proportion of those who were diseased or suffering from other disabilities than the records apparently show. I think there is some criticism to be directed 
to the medical officers in the three armed services who admitted these men. I had an example of one man who was certainly away over the age limit specified during the first year of the war, who got as far as England and was then returned to this country. In speaking to him in an effort to help him I said, "It is perfectly obvious, sir, that you have one eye that is bad; I would judge that probably you cannot see out of that eye." He admitted that this was correct. Then I said, "The question naturally arises, how did you get by?" The suggestion was that he had memorized the chart and was able to fool the medical officer.
Did he falsify his age?

I have not the slightest
doubt he did, and in that he was aided and abetted by others in the armed forces, a practice which is not unknown to old soldiers. He was a fine patriotic citizen, but the fact that he was permitted to pass, I believe, three medical examinations before he was eventually sent back to this country as unfit for service raised doubts in my mind as to the propriety of the medical examinations that are given brave men who offer their lives in the service of their country. I think the figures quoted disprove the foundation for the argument advanced by the hon. member for Swift Current. But it was not with respect to that that I rose to question the minister. I was prompted by the question directed to the minister by the hon. member for Edmonton East. I did not know this department had a wing of the civic hospital, which, apparently, it built and operates or to which it contributes. In Calgary we are fortunate in having what we are led to believe will be, when completed, one of the most modern and most completely equipped hospitals to be found anywhere in Canada or perhaps on this continent, for all of which we are duly grateful and appreciative. I commend the minister and his department for having provided, even at this late date, a fine hospital for our pensioners. I think it was a disgrace that the building on 8th avenue should have been used as a hospital all these years; I am sure the rents paid would have been sufficient to build two or three first class hospitals.
I come now to a question which has bothered me, as a result of the discussion which has been precipitated here by hon. members from the fair city of Toronto, in regard to the location of these hospitals. I was of opinion not only that the hospital in Calgary was badly located from every point of view, but that the new hospital might properly have

War Appropriation-Pensions and National Health
been located where I, as a layman, naturally would think a hospital should be situated- in some place with broad grounds, away from the noise, dust, smoke and distraction of city life. But every doubt or misgiving that I had in regard to the location of the new hospital in Calgary was answered, to my satisfaction at least, by one consideration, namely, the representations of the pensioners themselves. When the Canadian Legion and the representatives of these invalid soldiers come forward and say, "We want a hospital, not out in the foothills, not out on the shores of a lake but as centrally located as we can get it, so that we may have access to the movies and to the attractions afforded by a downtown district, where we will be readily accessible to our friends and relatives who want to come and see us," that settles it for me. When I am told by the men and women whose duty it is to wait upon these soldiers that the men undergoing treatment want to be downtown in the city, for the reasons I have mentioned, I say that where the soldiers want it is where it shall be, as far as I am concerned. I believe that that consideration should outweigh all others, because if the soldier undergoing treatment would'be unhappy or lonesome, no matter how beautiful the grounds might be in some remote district, where his friends would have difficulty in getting to him and he would not see the people going by, then I say the wish of the soldiers should determine the location of the hospital. I should like to hear some expression from the minister as to what the soldiers undergoing treatment in Christie Street hospital have to say with regard to the location of the hospital and what they would say if, as has been advocated, the hospital should be located six or eight miles from downtown Toronto.
I should like the minister to state also the policy of his department in regard to the suggestion I have heard enunciated and which I would understand has been carried out in some cases at least, that at certain points his department cooperates with the municipal authorities in building additions to civic hospitals, and under what circumstances that will be done, if at all. I am reminded now that at the time the new hospital in Calgary was being considered, very strong representations were made to the department that it might well cooperate with the city of Calgary in building a new civic hospital, so that I should like to know whether there is any principle underlying the policy of the department
of not going into partnership with municipal authorities in the construction of hospitals for pensioners.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: In the first place the policy of the department is to utilize as far as possible the hospitals they have had through the years, and to extend them, because as a rule the men themselves prefer those hospitals to any others. In the second place, where the pension department has no hospital facilities at the present time, we may agree, as we have done in two instances already-in Edmonton and in Ottawa-to take steps to extend existing hospital facilities in these places. That step is in contemplation at one other point at the present time, but that only happens where there are no hospitals of our own as such,

I cannot let the argument of the hon. member for Calgary West go unanswered. He suggests that my argument in favour of the insurance principle is not borne out, because some figures might seem to indicate that medical officers employed by the government may not have performed their duties thoroughly in examining men who offered themselves for enlistment. I submit that his very statement, accepting his inferences as correct, places the onus still more squarely upon the government and this country. What is the position? In a moment of patriotism a man comes to offer himself for enlistment in the service of his country. Such men know that if they were accepted they will have to give up their ordinary work and leave their homes. I do not think it is possible for any person to say what will be the result of service in a theatre of War, particularly to those who were not examined thoroughly enough to have any defects discovered; but I believe the principle should be recognized that the onus is on the country to say to that man, when he appears to enlist, "You are well enough to undergo the sendee we expect of you" or, after examination, "You are not fit to undergo that, and therefore you can not enlist and must return to your civilian environment and occupation". But if we as a country accept the man in a given category, despite the fact that the medical officers who examined him may have been careless, or even derelict in their duty, I think the onus is upon us, and that no man can thereafter say just how much that man's disability has been increased by reason of active service. Certainly it would be unfair to the individual to say, "We made a mistake; we were careless in our examination. We should never have accepted you. And because of that we refuse to accept the responsibility of recognizing that your
4S18	COMMONS
War Appropriation-Pensions and National Health
duties may have added to your physical disabilities." So that I do not think .the argument advanced by the hon. member for Calgary West in any way changes the principle I urged1 upon the minister as one which should be recognized in dealing with those who enlist in our armed forces.

In the discussion I have heard I agree with the hon. member for Swift Current. However, that is not what I rose particularly to say. I understand the minister has allowed a great deal of latitude in the discussion of this item, and as I have been unable to be in the house because of other matters perhaps I might be permitted to say a few words on another problem. I wanted to bring the attention of the minister again to a condition which exists by reason of the number of medical men taken into the army, particularly from our rural districts in the west.
I have heard medical men say that if our armed services had one medical service; if it were united instead of being divided four ways, there would be ample medical attention for both the armed forces and the civilian population. I know that during the winter the minister made every effort to meet the conditions in the rural areas, and for that I wish to thank him. However, his efforts were unsuccessful. I am thinking of the situation which applied in my own constituency at Lucky Lake, a very large area in which there are some 7,000 people and two or three hospitals, but no doctor, no nurse and no medical aid of any description. During last winter, which was a bitter and a long one, there were occasions when people were actually unable to get medical assistance before they died. This is a very serious situation, and one which exists not only in my own province, but also in other provinces, including that represented by the minister himself. I am wondering if some plan cannot be worked out whereby aid could be given to the rural districts to relieve this situation. It is indeed a terrible situation when we find people living twenty, thirty and forty miles away from a doctor, sometimes in communities where there are hospitals, and yet unable to obtain attention when that attention is needed.
I am not criticizing the minister, because I know that in the past winter he did endeavour to relieve the situation, but without success. It is true that, owing to the fact that medical men have moved away from some of the cities, others have gone in to take their places. I am told by medical men -of course, usually by the well-established ones-in these large cities that there are quan-

titles of doctors in the cities, and that the men who are coming in are really not needed in those areas.
One hesitates to suggest that anything in the nature of compulsion should be exercised. However, we are exercising compulsion in respect of men required to join the army, and it seems to me that if voluntary efforts fail we shall have to work out some scheme of compulsion applied to medical men and nurses, so that they may be placed in districts where they are needed, districts in which the emoluments and living conditions may not be quite so attractive. Would the minister say a word on this point?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
I thank the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar for bringing this matter to the attention of the committee. We had some correspondence in the winter months about the situation in Saskatchewan. Since that time I have been reading some dispatches describing the condition in the United States. I find that the situation in parts of that country was much more intense than it has been in Canada. The trouble has been, first of all, on account of doctors moving away from the country to the oities. That difficulty is pronounced. For instance, the city of Winnipeg, with the greatest number of medical enlistments of any part of Canada, has actually more doctors at the present time than it had before the war. The medical procurement board has been conducting a national survey, as my hon. friend knows. I understand that the report, has nearly been completed or is about to be completed, and that it deals with this situation. However, I have not yet seen the report myself, and I do not know what has been recommended.
In Australia compulsion has been exercised, giving medical doctors the rank of major. They have been compelled to serve in districts where they were required. Similar action has been taken in Great Britain, so that doctors might be moved to certain places, and I understand such action is about to be taken in the United States. That may be the only remedy in Canada, unless we succeed in meeting the situation in another way.
Our conditions have been greatly helped by defence service doctors who assist us in the hospitals. But the greatest difficulty has been experienced in remote areas, like Lucky Lake. However, I shall look into the report on the matter and see if there is any further information I can give my hon. friend at a later date.

Will the minister make a statement with respect to the future policy

of the government in connection with the Colonel Belcher hospital?

I understand it is under
lease?

Item agreed to.
Treatment, Royal Canadian Mounted Police,

Since this appropriation of $110,000 is a war appropriation, I would assume it does not apply to the regular members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police force. We know that following the outbreak of the war many of the old exmembers of the force were invited to rejoin the service for a period of one year at a time. Then, certain special constables were taken on strength to act as guards. Does this appropriation apply only to men who have been taken on temporarily since the outbreak of war?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: That is more or less correct. That is the explanation why there is a vote in the war appropriation measure. There is another one in the civil estimates.
On what basis is assistance given to those individuals so employed?

I understand that the field men, in my part of the country at least, or supervisors of the soldiers' settlement board, carry on investigational work for the dependents' allowance board. In certain instances they are given the authority to appoint representatives in various communities to make investigations for them. I understand that these special investigators are paid on the basis of so much per investigation. I am not satisfied with that arrangement. I feel that a supervisor for the soldiers' settlement board has his hands full with soldier settlement work. I do not wish to cast any reflection upon any individual supervisor, but in many cases these 
men have developed a certain type of mentality as a result of having dealt with soldier settler problems. They have built up certain prejudices from dealing with returned soldiers, and very frequently this is reflected in the treatment recommended for applicants for dependents' allowances. I have had considerable correspondence with the minister regarding air raid precautions. With all due respect, there should be some revision in central Canada of this work. The government has given a lot of money to the provinces and municipalities for
equipment in connection with A.RP. work. No doubt they have done a great deal of good in connection with the war so far, especially on the two coasts and on the St. Lawrence, but in central Canada they have gone too far altogether with blackouts of one hour's duration. We had one in Toronto on the zero night, January 27. In England, which has now almost achieved air supremacy, and where there was a real need for air raid precautions, Mr. Morrison, the Home Secretary, made a statement in the British House of Commons last January that blackouts were to be curtailed and more lights permitted on the streets.
I have had a lot of correspondence with the minister regarding the very elaborate system of blackouts that we have had in the central cities in Canada, in the Toronto and Ottawa districts, and other places in the province of Ontario where there is now practcally no danger. Some people have been talking for years of an invasion by air from the north, from Hudson bay. I see that Mayor LaGuardia, who is on the joint defence board, made a statement in Edmonton to-day that there is no danger now of air raids from Japan on this continent. What he knows about it I do not know, but he is a member of the famous joint defence board. What I say is that this air raid precautions work should have been under the control of the military authorities in the different military divisions if there were any grave danger to the civilian population. When the war started I doubt whether there was a gas mask in many of the districts in Canada.
I think we should have a statement from the government with respect to these hour-long black-outs, which take up so much of the time of the police force and take county judges away from their judicial duties. Some of the police force spend two-thirds or all of their time on this work of air raid precautions, so much so that they have not the time to attend to their proper functions of protecting the civilian population, with the result that several people have been killed on the highways by cars travelling at excessive rates of speed when there were not sufficient police to attend to their heavy civilian and other police duties. But now those in authority are beginning to hearken to the call. Queen's Park has announced that the black-outs are to be cut down to twenty minutes or a half-hour. I think the minister should amend this order in council in this district and make a statement about the whole thing. What is the necessity in central Canada for these long black-outs which cause a lot of suffering to people in hospitals and
