speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
If I may reply first to the hon. member for Broadview, possibly some other people share his opinions, but I certainly do not. I would like him to recall the early days of the war when the cry was practically unanimous that we were not doing enough in civilian defence, and even a year ago, faced with a menacing situation, the department which is responsible for this work was criticized for not having made ample preparations. Under the most efficient and devoted work of the late Doctor Manion, an organization has been built up of one-quarter of a million splendid voluntary workers throughout the dominion, men and women who are rendering magnificent service, and who should have the eternal gratitude of the Canadian people for the work they are doing outside of their regular working hours for the most part and doing it without any compensation whatsoever and with very little glory attached to it, their satisfaction being the knowledge that they are rendering a fine service to their country.
Most of the equipment that will be required is provided for in this year's estimates. I anticipate that later on the same amount of equipment will not be required as justifies the amount here. This equipment was ordered last year and has not yet been delivered.
In regard to the second point mentioned by the hon. member for Broadview, I agree with him as to the length of the black-outs. I think an hour's black-out is too long, but that is left entirely to the provincial authorities. There is no interference from the director's office in Ottawa in regard to the length of the black-out. The authority is delegated to the provincial premier or the provincial attorney-general as the case may be, whose officers are in liaison with the defences services. They arrange a time which they consider prudent for holding a black-out. I understand that in Toronto they have decided that in future the black-outs will not be of such long duration as the last one, w'hich lasted one hour.

I appreciate what the
minister has said. So far so good. But if the minister wants to delegate these powers to the provinces and give them such wide jurisdiction over the liberty of the subject in time of war, he must take the responsibility for it. I can tell him this, that placards are put up in every residential district in every municipality in central Canada which are issued, according to the wording on them, under the authority of the minister. These long black-outs may be all right on the Pacific coast and along the St. Lawrence and the Atlantic seaboard, but there is not the same danger now in central Canada, and whoever it was announced that there might be an invasion by air from the north from Hudson bay had no basis for his apprehension, because there are no enemy bases there. A lot of it was simply ridiculous. I can tell you this, as a former chairman of the police commission of Toronto, that the police were so much occupied1 with all this federal work that a large number of them did not have the time to attend to their own police duties. Mounted police and others werd so engaged, with the result that there was no way of checking reckless speeding all over Toronto district. Cars and trucks were passing my house all night long; they were going fifty to sixty miles an hour, and people were being knocked down and injured all over the city, while a great many police were away on this work. I ask only for more reasonable enforcement in central Canada. The minister is well meaning and the A.R.P. people are very good citizens, but they could be given more useful work of other kinds as well in the cities of central Canada such as Toronto and Hamilton, than they are doing.
As regards the order in council relating to black-outs, people of all classes have been summoned and some of them fined. Some of the fines are so large as to be ridiculous as well as inequitable. In the Toronto district the order was enforced to the letter; they were peeping in keyholes and back kitchens and all that sort of thing, whereas in England some of the streets and cars and buses are now lit up. Many people were haled to court. One of our own ministers of the crown was summoned to the police court and fined. A lot of this is not at all reasonable. I do not believe the minister himself believes in it. It has gone altogether too far. All the dominion did was hand over a whole lot of equipment. Now, some of these A.R.P. gentlemen want an increase of gasoline. It is time to make the black-out regulation more reasonable in central Canada,

There are some questions I should like to ask about those respirators, or, as I think I am correct in calling them, gas masks. How many gas masks or respirators



War Appropriation-National Health
are there in the country? Who supplied them? How much was paid to each firm that supplied those respirators? Where are they kept? What steps are being taken to distribute them? Who is looking after the distribution?
When I was in Saint John about three weeks ago I saw some respirators or gas masks, which I presume were the ones that the government had obtained, on sale in the windows of some stores, and if I recollect correctly, the price was $1.75 each.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: It is $155.

To-day I received a letter from the common clerk of the city of Saint John enclosing a resolution which was passed by the common council of the city of Saint John on the 8th instant. I should like to bring it to the attention of the minister; it has to do with these gas masks or respirators:
Resolved that the federal government be advised that the common council feel that respirators should be supplied free to all citizens of vulnerable areas, and that therefore neither the city of Saint John nor its citizens should be required to meet the expense incurred by the supplying of respirators but that all Canadians should share equally in this cost.
I bring this resolution to the attention of the minister in the hope that he will give it his serious consideration. I believe, although I am not speaking positively, that in Great Britain the gas masks or respirators were furnished free of charge to the citizens of certain districts. Why should the citizens of this country living in vulnerable areas be compelled to purchase these gas masks? It would appear that the government has spent, as I say, $2,500,000 for these masks, and they are not required by all Canadian citizens. There is some need for them possibly for citizens who are living in certain areas of Canada, but it seems hardly fair that in those districts where they may be required the government should ask citizens to purchase them at $1.25 each, when in other parts of Canada they will not be required. It is of course extremely difficult for many people with large families to purchase these masks at that price. It means that people who are well to do will get them while others who are not so well off will have to go without. The principle is not fair.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
This matter was carefully considered, and the solution adopted was to issue the masks free to those who could not afford to purchase them but to make them available at the price mentioned to those who could. The idea behind H was that greater care would be taken of the

masks if people had the privilege of paying a small amount for them, if they could afford it. As to how many there are in Canada, I would rather not answer that question at the present time, if my hon. friend does not mind. They were supplied to us through the Department of Munitions and Supply. I do not know the source, but I will find that out. They are principally on both coasts and in reserve at the present time, those that have not been distributed. They have been distributed free to voluntary workers in the organization, and a certain number of civilians. It may be necessary to have a change in policy.
